intake_responses.business_description: I sell second-hand clothes, what we call mivumba, here in Owino. I buy bales from the importers and then sort them and sell to my customers. I mostly deal in ladies' dresses and children's wear.
intake_responses.customers: My customers are mostly women from around Kampala who come looking for cheap but good quality clothes. Some are small resellers who buy from me and take to their villages. Many come on market days.
intake_responses.competitors: Eh, there are so many of us selling mivumba in Owino, you can't count. The person next to me sells the same dresses. So sometimes it comes down to who calls the customer first or who gives a better price.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I make my money from selling the clothes. When I open a good bale I can make maybe 300,000 to 400,000 shillings profit on it, but a bad bale can even give me loss.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest problem is the bales themselves. When I buy from the supplier I cannot see inside properly, so sometimes I pay 500,000 for a bale and half of it is torn or old-fashioned things nobody wants. I lose money and I can't blame the supplier because that is how the business is.
intake_responses.current_plan: For now I am trying to save so I can buy directly from a bigger importer where maybe the bales are graded better. I am also thinking of learning which brands sell fast so I choose my bales more carefully.

intake_responses.business_description: I run a poultry farm just outside Gulu town. I keep layers for eggs, right now about 800 birds. I sell eggs to shops and restaurants in Gulu and sometimes I sell the old hens off when they stop laying.
intake_responses.customers: My main customers are retail shops, hotels and some schools around Gulu. A few individuals also come to the farm directly to buy trays of eggs at a better price.
intake_responses.competitors: There are other poultry farmers here and also eggs that come all the way from Kampala and Jinja by lorry. Those Kampala eggs are sometimes cheaper even though transport is far, and that confuses me.
intake_responses.revenue_source: My income is from selling eggs, mostly by the tray. When birds are laying well I collect maybe 20 trays a day. I also earn a bit from selling manure to crop farmers.
intake_responses.main_challenge: Feed is killing me. The price of feed keeps going up and the quality is not consistent, so sometimes my birds reduce laying and I don't know if it's the feed, the weather or disease. When laying drops I still have to feed them the same, so I'm spending without earning.
intake_responses.current_plan: I want to start mixing my own feed using maize and silverfish from the farmers here to cut costs. I am also thinking of getting a vet to check the birds regularly instead of only when they fall sick.

intake_responses.business_description: I have a small juice bar in Wandegeya near the university. I make fresh juice from passion fruit, mango, watermelon and also smoothies. Students are my main people because they like the cold drinks.
intake_responses.customers: Mostly Makerere students and young workers around Wandegeya. They come in the afternoon when it's hot and on weekends. Some order through boda when they are in their hostels.
intake_responses.competitors: There are two other juice places near me and also the shops selling bottled sodas and packed juice which are cheaper. The students sometimes just buy a soda because it's 1,500 and my juice is 3,000.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I earn from selling the juices and smoothies over the counter. On a good day I can sell 60 to 70 cups. I also take some orders for events like small birthday parties.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My sales completely die during the university holidays. When students go home Wandegeya becomes quiet and I can go from 70 cups to maybe 15 a day. I still pay rent and my worker so those months I eat into whatever I saved, and it's hard to plan.
intake_responses.current_plan: I am thinking of finding customers who are not students, like offices nearby, so I have steady sales even in holidays. I also want to start delivering to homes using the boda guys through mobile money orders.

intake_responses.business_description: I am a wholesaler in Kikuubo. I sell household items like buckets, plastic plates, jerrycans and basins in bulk to retailers who come from upcountry. I buy the goods from importers and Nairobi sometimes.
intake_responses.customers: My customers are shopkeepers from towns like Masaka, Mbarara and even DRC side. They buy in cartons and dozens and then go resell. So I don't deal much with the final person using the bucket.
intake_responses.competitors: Kikuubo is packed with people selling exactly the same plastics. The competition is on price, and some of the big guys import container loads so they sell cheaper than I even buy. That's my struggle.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I make money on the margin per carton. It's a small margin like 5 to 10 percent but I move large volumes so it adds up. Most of my sales are cash but some trusted customers I give on short credit.
intake_responses.main_challenge: Cash flow is my headache because some customers take goods on credit and then delay paying, especially the upcountry ones. Meanwhile my suppliers want cash upfront for the next stock. So I get stuck where I have money on paper but no cash to restock, and I miss good deals.
intake_responses.current_plan: I am trying to reduce credit and only give to customers I know very well. I am also saving to have a reserve so that when a good import deal comes I can pay cash and get the lower price.

intake_responses.business_description: I cook and sell food in Lira town, mainly local food like posho, matoke, beans, groundnut sauce and meat for lunch. I have a small place where workers come to eat. I open from morning until evening.
intake_responses.customers: My customers are boda riders, market people and workers from the shops around. They come for lunch mostly between 1 and 3 o'clock. Some come every day so I know them well.
intake_responses.competitors: There are other food places around here doing the same food. The competition is who cooks tasty food and who is fair with the plate size. Some undercut me by giving smaller meat pieces but cheaper price.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I earn from each plate of food I sell, around 4,000 to 6,000 depending on what they eat. On a busy day I can serve maybe 50 people. I buy fresh ingredients each morning from the market.
intake_responses.main_challenge: The prices of food in the market keep jumping, especially matoke and meat, but my customers get annoyed if I raise my plate price. So when the market is expensive I either lose money or I reduce the portion and then customers complain. I am always squeezed in the middle.
intake_responses.current_plan: I want to try buying some things like beans and posho flour in bulk when they are cheap and store them. For matoke I am thinking of getting a farmer who supplies me directly so I skip the market middlemen.

intake_responses.business_description: I repair phones and sell accessories like screen protectors, chargers and earphones in a small stall in Jinja. I do things like changing screens, software issues and unlocking phones. I learned it at a vocational school.
intake_responses.customers: Mostly young people and students, and workers who have broken screens. Some come because their phone won't switch on or has a virus. I get maybe 8 to 12 customers a day.
intake_responses.competitors: There are many small repair guys in Jinja and some do it cheaper because they use fake or lower quality parts. Customers sometimes go to them, then come back to me when the cheap screen spoils again.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I earn from the repair labour and from selling the spare parts and accessories. A screen replacement can give me 20,000 to 40,000 profit depending on the phone model.
intake_responses.main_challenge: Getting genuine spare parts is very hard. My supplier in Kampala sometimes sends me screens that are labelled original but they are not, and I only find out after I've installed it and the customer comes back complaining. It's ruining my reputation and I have to redo work for free.
intake_responses.current_plan: I am looking for a more trusted supplier even if it means paying more, because losing customers is worse. I also want to start giving a warranty so customers trust my work over the cheaper guys.

intake_responses.business_description: I sell shoes in Mbale town, both new and slightly used ones. I deal in ladies' shoes, men's leather shoes and children's shoes. I have a stall in the market and I also lay out some on the veranda.
intake_responses.customers: All kinds of people, but mostly women buying for themselves and their children. Parents come a lot when school is opening because children need new shoes. I also get people preparing for weddings and functions.
intake_responses.competitors: Plenty of shoe sellers in Mbale, and there's also the new shops selling imported shoes in the arcades. Those arcade ones look fancy so some customers prefer them even though mine are cheaper and good.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I earn from selling each pair, with margins from about 5,000 up to 20,000 on the better shoes. My sales spike at school opening and festive seasons but are slow in between.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My money is tied up in stock that isn't moving. I bought many pairs in sizes and styles that customers are not asking for, and now that capital is just sitting on the shelf. Meanwhile the fast-moving sizes I run out of quickly and can't restock because my cash is stuck in the slow stock.
intake_responses.current_plan: I want to sell off the slow shoes even at cost just to free up money. Then I plan to be more careful, buying more of the sizes and styles that actually move fast instead of guessing.

intake_responses.business_description: I do agro-processing, mainly maize milling. I buy maize from farmers around Mbarara, dry it and mill it into maize flour which I package and sell as posho flour. I sell in different bag sizes.
intake_responses.customers: I sell to schools, small shops and some individuals who buy the smaller packets. Schools are big buyers because they feed many students posho. I also supply a few restaurants.
intake_responses.competitors: There are bigger millers with branded flour and better packaging, and they have machines that produce cleaner flour. My flour is good but my packaging looks local, so some shops prefer the branded ones.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I earn from the milling and selling the flour. The margin depends on the maize buying price at harvest time. I make more when I buy maize cheap during harvest and sell flour when prices rise.
intake_responses.main_challenge: Power outages are really hurting me. When UMEME cuts power my mill just stops and I have farmers' maize waiting and orders I can't fulfil. I bought a generator but the fuel makes each bag so expensive that I lose my margin. So I'm stuck between missing orders or milling at a loss.
intake_responses.current_plan: I am saving to buy a bigger generator that is more efficient on fuel, or maybe look into solar. I am also trying to schedule my milling to run mostly when power is stable, but that's hard to predict.

intake_responses.business_description: I run a salon in Kalerwe. I do hair plaiting, weaves, braids, washing and treatment, and also some nail work. I have one girl helping me. I trained in a beauty school before starting.
intake_responses.customers: Mostly women from the neighbourhood, market women and young ladies. They come especially on weekends and month end when they have been paid. Weddings and functions bring extra work too.
intake_responses.competitors: There are so many salons in Kalerwe, almost every corner. Some new ones open and offer very low prices to pull customers, so people move to whoever is cheaper that week.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I earn from each service, like braiding can be 20,000 to 50,000 depending on the style. I also sell some hair products and extensions to the customers who need them.
intake_responses.main_challenge: I struggle to keep customers coming back regularly. A customer comes, I do a good job, but then she disappears for two months or goes to another salon. I don't understand if it's my prices, the waiting time, or just that people are broke. My chairs are empty on weekdays and packed only on weekends.
intake_responses.current_plan: I am thinking of starting a system where regular customers get a small discount so they keep coming back. I also want to use WhatsApp to remind them and post my styles so they book appointments instead of just walking in.

intake_responses.business_description: I ride a boda-boda in Gulu and I also help other riders. I actually own two motorcycles now, one I ride myself and one I gave to another rider who pays me daily. I carry passengers and do deliveries.
intake_responses.customers: My passengers are everyday people going to work, market, hospital. For deliveries, some shops call me to take goods to customers. I have some regular clients who call me directly on my phone.
intake_responses.competitors: There are very many boda riders in Gulu, and now those app ones and also the fuel guzzlers charging small money. Everyone is fighting for the same passengers at the stage.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I earn from the fares I ride and the daily deposit the second rider gives me for using my bike. Fuel and repairs take a big chunk though. On a normal day I make maybe 30,000 net for myself.
intake_responses.main_challenge: The rider I hired to use my second bike is not consistent. Some days he brings the full daily deposit, other days he says business was bad or the bike had a problem, and I can't verify. I suspect he's cheating me but I have no way to track how much he actually made. I'm losing income from my own asset.
intake_responses.current_plan: I want to set a fixed daily amount he must bring no matter what, like a rental agreement, so I'm not depending on his honesty. I'm also thinking of maybe using a tracker or agreeing on clear rules in writing.

intake_responses.business_description: I sell and install solar systems, mostly small home solar kits with lights and phone charging, and some bigger ones for businesses. I do the supply, installation and after-sale service. I operate around Naalya and go upcountry for bigger jobs.
intake_responses.customers: My customers are people in areas without good power, and also town people who want backup during outages. Businesses like shops and clinics that lose money during blackouts are good clients.
intake_responses.competitors: There are big solar companies with financing options and there are also cheap fake solar products flooding the market. The fake ones are cheaper so some customers buy those and get disappointed, which spoils the trust in solar generally.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I earn from the markup on the solar equipment and the installation fees. Bigger systems give me better margins. I sometimes get maintenance contracts which give steady small income.
intake_responses.main_challenge: The upfront cost blocks many customers. People want solar but a good system is like 800,000 to 2 million shillings, and they can't pay all at once. The big companies offer pay-in-instalments through mobile money, but I don't have the capital to give customers products and wait for them to pay over months.
intake_responses.current_plan: I am exploring whether I can partner with a company that does the financing so I just do the sales and installation. Or I find a way to get stock on credit from a supplier so I can offer small instalment plans to customers.

intake_responses.business_description: I make and sell chapati and rolex in Owino market area. I have a stand where I fry chapati and eggs, and I make rolex, chapati with cabbage and other fillings. I start early morning for the workers' breakfast.
intake_responses.customers: Market vendors, porters, boda riders and shoppers passing by. Morning is breakfast time and evening people buy rolex on their way home. I sell fast because it's cheap food, 1,000 to 3,000.
intake_responses.competitors: There are other chapati stands nearby and everyone's chapati looks the same. The difference is who is faster, who's clean, and who gives a bigger chapati. Sometimes it's just where you're positioned that decides who gets the customer.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I earn from selling chapati and rolex. My margin per piece is small but I sell high volume. On a good day I use like two big basins of dough. Wheat flour and cooking oil are my main costs.
intake_responses.main_challenge: The price of cooking oil and wheat flour keeps going up but I can't increase my chapati price because customers are so price sensitive, a rolex must stay at a certain price or they walk away. My margin keeps shrinking and some days I wonder if I'm even making profit after buying everything.
intake_responses.current_plan: I want to buy flour and oil in bulk with other vendors together so we get a lower price. I'm also thinking of adding higher value items like a special rolex with more fillings that I can charge more for to the customers who can afford it.

intake_responses.business_description: I sell clothes and shoes online, mostly through Instagram and WhatsApp. I import ladies' fashion, dresses, shoes and bags and post them online, then deliver by boda around Kampala. I don't have a physical shop.
intake_responses.customers: Young working women and university students who like fashionable things and prefer shopping from their phones. They order through DM, pay mobile money and I send by boda or they pick from an agreed point.
intake_responses.competitors: There are so many online clothing pages now, everyone is importing and selling on Instagram. Many of them post nicer photos and have more followers, so they get more orders even when we sell similar things.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I earn from the markup on each item. I buy from Kampala importers or order from Turkey and China. Delivery fees I pass to the customer. My margins are decent but I have to keep buying new stock to stay trendy.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest issue is people who order and then cancel or don't pick up. They tell me to buy or reserve an item, I hold it, then they go quiet or say they changed their mind after I've paid a boda to go deliver. I lose the delivery money and I'm stuck with reserved stock I turned other buyers away from.
intake_responses.current_plan: I want to start requiring a deposit through mobile money before I reserve or deliver anything. I'm also thinking of building trust with reviews and clear policies posted on my page so serious buyers know I'm not playing.

intake_responses.business_description: I have a fish farm in Fort Portal area with earthen ponds where I raise tilapia and some catfish. I grow them and sell when they mature, both to traders and directly to people. I've been doing this for about four years.
intake_responses.customers: Fish traders who take to markets, some restaurants and hotels, and individuals who come to buy fresh fish at the farm. Demand is good because people love fresh tilapia here.
intake_responses.competitors: There's fish coming from Lake George and Lake Edward which is cheaper because it's caught, not farmed. My farmed fish costs more to produce so I have to convince people mine is fresher and safer.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I earn when I harvest and sell the mature fish, so my income comes in big lumps every few months rather than daily. Between harvests I have expenses like fish feed but no income coming in.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My income timing is a serious problem. I only earn money when I harvest, which is every four to six months, but I spend on feed every single week. So between harvests I'm always broke and sometimes I'm forced to harvest fish early before they reach good size, which means I sell them small and cheap and lose money.
intake_responses.current_plan: I'm thinking of stocking ponds at different times so I can harvest something every month instead of all at once. I also want to add smoked fish so I can preserve and sell over time instead of dumping everything fresh at harvest.

intake_responses.business_description: I run a small general shop in Soroti selling household basics like soap, sugar, salt, cooking oil, matchboxes, airtime and mobile money. I'm the shop people around here run to for everyday small needs.
intake_responses.customers: The people in my neighbourhood, they come daily for small quantities like a cup of sugar or one bar of soap. Many buy small because they don't have much money at once. I also do a lot of mobile money transactions.
intake_responses.competitors: There are two other similar shops within walking distance and a bigger supermarket in town. The supermarket has lower prices on some things but people still come to me for the small quantities and because I'm nearby and give some on credit.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I earn small margins on the goods and I earn commission on the mobile money and airtime. The mobile money actually brings good steady income if I keep enough float. Goods bring more but slowly.
intake_responses.main_challenge: The neighbours keep buying on credit and my book is full of names who owe me. I feel bad refusing because they're my neighbours and they'll get offended, but this credit is eating my capital. Some take long to pay, some never pay, and meanwhile I struggle to restock and keep enough mobile money float.
intake_responses.current_plan: I want to slowly reduce credit and maybe set a limit per person. I'm also thinking of separating my mobile money float completely from the shop money so at least that side keeps running even when the credit book is bad.

intake_responses.business_description: I run an IT training and computer services center in Kampala. We teach basic computer skills, packages like Word and Excel, graphic design, and we also do printing, photocopying, typing and internet services. Mostly we serve students and job seekers.
intake_responses.customers: Students who need computer certificates for jobs, people who come to type documents, print, or do online applications. We get a lot around exam and application seasons. Some companies send staff for training.
intake_responses.competitors: There are many computer schools and internet cafes now, and honestly smartphones have reduced the internet cafe business because people browse on their phones. Free YouTube tutorials also make some people skip paying for training.
intake_responses.revenue_source: We earn from training fees, printing and photocopying, typing services and internet. Training brings bigger amounts but comes in intakes, while printing and photocopy is small but daily.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My whole model is being squeezed by smartphones and free online learning. Fewer people pay for internet because they have data on their phones, and some young people say they'll just learn computer stuff from YouTube for free. My training enrollment is dropping each intake and I don't know if I should change what I teach or how.
intake_responses.current_plan: I'm thinking of teaching more advanced skills that people can't easily just YouTube, like proper graphic design or data skills that employers want. I also want to offer online job application help and government portal services which people still need done properly.

intake_responses.business_description: I'm a tailor in Wandegeya. I make dresses, gomesis, school uniforms and I also do repairs and alterations. I have two sewing machines and I take in orders from customers who bring their material.
intake_responses.customers: Ladies who want custom dresses and gomesis for functions, parents needing school uniforms, and walk-ins needing quick repairs or altering trousers and dresses. Weddings and church functions bring good work.
intake_responses.competitors: Wandegeya has many tailors, and there's also ready-made imported clothes which are sometimes cheaper than sewing new. Some customers just buy ready-made instead of tailoring because it's faster.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I earn from the sewing charges per garment, more for complex ones like gomesis. Uniforms come in bulk during school opening. Repairs are small money but frequent.
intake_responses.main_challenge: I keep failing to deliver on time and customers get angry. When I get many orders at once, especially before a big function season, I promise everyone a date and then I can't finish because it's just me and one machine sometimes breaks down. Losing customers over late delivery hurts because word spreads that I delay.
intake_responses.current_plan: I want to hire and train an assistant so I can handle more orders, but I'm scared of the wage cost in slow months. I'm also thinking of being honest and giving realistic dates instead of over-promising just to get the order.

intake_responses.business_description: I sell electronics in Gulu, things like phones, phone accessories, radios, speakers, extension cables and rechargeable lamps. I have a small shop in the market area. I buy my stock from Kampala.
intake_responses.customers: Young people buying phones and accessories, and villagers coming to town who buy radios, torches and solar lamps to take back home. Speakers sell a lot when there are functions and during festive season.
intake_responses.competitors: There are other electronics shops in Gulu and the ones in town with bigger displays and newer phone models. Customers who want the latest phones sometimes go to those or even order from Kampala directly online.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I earn from the markup on each item. Phones give small margin but accessories like chargers, earphones and cases give better margins. Festive seasons boost my speaker and radio sales.
intake_responses.main_challenge: Transport and restocking from Kampala is my biggest struggle. Every time I go to Kampala to buy stock it costs me transport, lodging and time away from the shop, and if I misjudge what will sell I'm stuck with wrong stock far from where I bought it. I can't just quickly return or exchange like a Kampala trader can.
intake_responses.current_plan: I'm looking for a reliable Kampala supplier who can send me stock by bus so I don't always travel myself. I also want to keep better records of what sells fast so my buying trips are more accurate and I don't waste money on slow stock.

intake_responses.business_description: I sell fresh produce in Kalerwe market, mainly tomatoes, onions, greens, matoke and fruits. I buy from the trucks that bring produce from the villages very early morning and I sell throughout the day.
intake_responses.customers: Households, food vendors and small restaurants around Kalerwe come to buy from me. Restaurant people buy larger amounts, ordinary women buy for the day's cooking. Early morning is my busiest time.
intake_responses.competitors: The whole of Kalerwe is produce sellers, we're all selling tomatoes and onions side by side. When everyone has the same tomatoes the price goes down and we all lose. It's who the customer reaches first.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I earn from the difference between what I pay the truck and what I sell for. Fresh produce is risky because if it doesn't sell fast it rots and I lose. Good days I can clear everything, bad days I throw away.
intake_responses.main_challenge: Spoilage is eating my profit. Tomatoes and greens don't last, so if I buy plenty and the market is slow that day, by evening a lot has gone bad and I just throw it. But if I buy little to be safe, I run out when customers come and lose sales. I can never judge how much to buy and it changes every day.
intake_responses.current_plan: I want to find restaurant customers who order in advance so I know a portion is already sold before I buy. I'm also thinking of buying smaller and restocking during the day from other sellers instead of buying a big lot in the morning.

intake_responses.business_description: I own a restaurant in Mbarara serving local and some fast food. We do buffet lunch with matoke, rice, meat, chicken, and in the evening we do fried chicken, chips and roast meat. We have seating for about 40 people.
intake_responses.customers: Office workers and business people come for lunch, families and young people come in the evening and weekends. We also do a bit of takeaway and some small events and meetings booking the space.
intake_responses.competitors: There are several restaurants and newer fast food places in Mbarara, some with fancier setups and some doing delivery through apps. The younger customers like the ones with modern look and online ordering.
intake_responses.revenue_source: We earn from the food sales, lunch buffet is steady daily income, evening and weekend fast food gives good margins. Events and bookings bring extra lump sums occasionally.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My food costs are unpredictable and I can't figure out my actual profit. Some months I'm busy but at the end there's no money, and I can't tell if it's theft by staff, wastage in the kitchen, buying badly, or portions too big. Without knowing where the money leaks I keep guessing and can't fix it. I feel like I'm working hard for nothing.
intake_responses.current_plan: I want to start properly tracking what comes in and what goes out, maybe daily records of purchases and sales. I'm also thinking of standardizing portions and checking the store so I can see if the losses are from the kitchen or somewhere else.

intake_responses.business_description: I do catering for events in Mbale, weddings, introductions, parties and church functions. I cook the food, provide serving, and sometimes decorations. I have a small team I call when there's a big function.
intake_responses.customers: People organizing weddings, kwanjula ceremonies, birthday parties and corporate events. Most business comes through referrals from people who ate my food at a previous function and liked it.
intake_responses.competitors: There are other caterers in Mbale, some more established with bigger names and their own tents and chairs. Clients with big budgets go to those, so I mostly get the medium and smaller functions.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I earn per function based on the number of plates and the menu. Big weddings pay well but I have to spend a lot upfront to buy ingredients before the client fully pays. The season matters a lot too.
intake_responses.main_challenge: Clients pay me a small deposit then expect me to buy everything and finish the function before paying the balance, but some delay the balance for weeks after the event. So I'm always using my own money or borrowing to fund functions, and when a client delays payment I can't take the next job because my capital is stuck. It limits how many events I can handle.
intake_responses.current_plan: I want to change my terms so clients pay a bigger percentage before the function, enough to cover the ingredients. I'm also thinking of building a small working capital reserve so one delaying client doesn't stop my whole business.

intake_responses.business_description: I deal in stationery wholesale in Kikuubo, selling books, pens, exercise books, reams of paper and office supplies to shops and schools. I buy from the big importers and distributors and sell in bulk.
intake_responses.customers: Retail stationery shops from upcountry, schools buying supplies, and some offices. School term openings are my peak because everyone needs exercise books and pens for students.
intake_responses.competitors: Many stationery wholesalers in Kikuubo selling identical products, and the big manufacturers now sell directly to some big schools, cutting us out. So my margins are thin and I compete mostly on price and relationships.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I earn on volume with thin margins per item. Term opening seasons bring most of my yearly income in a few weeks. The rest of the year is slow and I'm mostly just covering rent.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My business is completely dependent on the three school terms. Around term opening I'm overwhelmed and even run short of stock and capital, then the moment term starts, sales crash and for two months I'm barely selling anything while still paying rent and staff. I'm either drowning or starving, never balanced, and it's hard to grow like this.
intake_responses.current_plan: I want to add products that sell throughout the year, like office supplies and printing paper for businesses, not just school items. I'm also thinking of borrowing strategically before term opening so I have enough stock to capture the peak I keep missing.

intake_responses.business_description: I run a bakery in Naalya making cakes, bread, cookies and pastries. I do custom cakes for birthdays and weddings, and I supply bread and snacks to a few nearby shops. I bake from a setup at home.
intake_responses.customers: People ordering celebration cakes, families around Naalya buying bread and snacks, and the shops I supply. A lot of cake orders come through Instagram and WhatsApp where I post my work.
intake_responses.competitors: There are many home bakers now, everyone with an oven is selling cakes on Instagram, and big bakeries supply cheaper bread. So cake prices are being pushed down and bread margins are tight against the big guys.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I earn from custom cake orders which have the best margins, and steady but smaller income from bread and snacks supply. Weekends and festive seasons bring the most cake orders.
intake_responses.main_challenge: I want to grow beyond baking from home but I'm stuck. My home oven and space can only handle so many orders, so I turn down business on busy weekends, but renting a proper commercial space and buying a bigger oven needs capital I don't have. I'm too big for home but too small to afford a real bakery, caught in the middle and unable to scale.
intake_responses.current_plan: I'm thinking of first hiring help and maybe getting one more oven to squeeze more out of my current space before jumping to rent. I also want to focus on the high-margin custom cakes and reduce the low-margin bread so I earn more per order without needing more space.

intake_responses.business_description: I do construction and metal fabrication in Jinja. I make metal doors, windows, gates, burglar bars and I also take small building and welding contracts. I have a workshop with welding machines and a couple of workers.
intake_responses.customers: People building houses who need doors, windows and gates, businesses needing security bars, and sometimes contractors who subcontract me for the metal parts of their projects. Word of mouth brings most jobs.
intake_responses.competitors: There are other fabricators in Jinja and some do the work cheaper by using thinner metal or rushing the finishing. Customers who only look at price go to them and then get poor quality that bends or rusts fast.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I earn per job based on the materials plus my labour and profit. Big gate and window contracts pay well but they come irregularly. Small welding repairs give quick small money in between.
intake_responses.main_challenge: Metal prices keep changing and I sometimes quote a customer a price, they take time to decide, and by the time they agree the price of iron has gone up so I either lose money or have to go back and ask for more which makes me look untrustworthy. Also power outages stop my welding, so I lose working days I can't recover, and workers I pay anyway.
intake_responses.current_plan: I want to put a short time limit on my quotations so prices are only valid for maybe a week, and factor in a buffer for material price rises. For power I'm considering a welding generator so a blackout doesn't cost me a whole working day and my workers' wages.

intake_responses.business_description: I grow and sell vegetables and also do a bit of poultry on my small piece of land near Mbale. Mainly I grow tomatoes, cabbages, sukuma wiki and onions, and I keep local chickens for eggs and meat. I sell in the Mbale market.
intake_responses.customers: Market vendors who buy my vegetables to resell, households, and some restaurants that buy greens and eggs. When I harvest cabbages, traders come and buy in bulk from the garden sometimes.
intake_responses.competitors: Many farmers around Mbale grow the same vegetables, so at harvest time the market is flooded and prices fall for everybody. When there's plenty of tomatoes, we practically give them away because they'll rot otherwise.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I earn from selling the vegetables at harvest and from eggs and chickens which give more regular smaller income. Vegetable income depends heavily on the market price at the time I harvest.
intake_responses.main_challenge: The problem is everyone harvests at the same time so prices collapse exactly when I have the most to sell. I put in all this work and money on seeds and fertilizer, then when my tomatoes are ready the whole market has tomatoes and the price is nothing, so I barely recover my costs. If I could sell when prices are high I'd do well, but the timing always works against me.
intake_responses.current_plan: I'm thinking of planting at off-seasons using some irrigation so I harvest when others don't and prices are higher. I also want to try simple value addition like drying vegetables or making them last longer so I'm not forced to sell everything the moment it's ready.

intake_responses.business_description: I sell second-hand clothes, what we call mivumba, here at Kalerwe. I buy bales of clothes and open them, then sort the good ones and price them. I have been doing this business for about five years now.
intake_responses.customers: My customers are mostly young people and working women who want nice clothes but cannot afford new ones from the boutiques. Many come in the evening after work when they are passing through the market.
intake_responses.competitors: Eh, we are so many selling mivumba here, maybe twenty stalls in my row alone. Everyone is opening bales so the prices keep going down as we compete for the same customers.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I make money from selling the clothes piece by piece. On a good day I can make maybe eighty thousand shillings, but it depends on what came in the bale.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My real problem is the bales themselves. When I buy a bale for like three hundred thousand, I don't know what is inside until I open it. Sometimes half the clothes are torn or old-fashioned and I cannot sell them, so I lose money on that same bale. But my supplier says all bales are mixed like that, so I don't know if it's bad luck or if I am being cheated.
intake_responses.current_plan: For now I just try to buy from different suppliers hoping one gives better quality. I also sometimes wash and iron the wrinkled ones to sell them better, but it takes a lot of my time.

intake_responses.business_description: I run a phone repair shop near the taxi park in Gulu. I fix screens, change batteries, and also unlock phones and install software for people. I trained in Kampala for one year before coming back home.
intake_responses.customers: My customers are ordinary people whose phones have fallen or the battery has died. Also boda riders who use their phones a lot, and some students from the nearby schools.
intake_responses.competitors: There are maybe four or five other repair guys around here. Some of them charge very little because they use cheap fake parts, so customers go to them first even though the parts fail quickly.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I earn from the repair labour and also from selling the parts like screens and batteries. Sometimes I buy and sell used phones too when I get a good deal.
intake_responses.main_challenge: The thing that confuses me is that I do good work with genuine parts, but customers complain I am expensive and go to the cheaper guys. Then when the cheap repair fails, some come back to me, but many just think all repairers are the same and blame me too. I can't tell if I should lower my prices or explain the quality better.
intake_responses.current_plan: Right now I give a small warranty of two weeks on my repairs to show my work is good. I am also thinking of stocking some cheaper parts as an option so I don't lose the price-sensitive customers.

intake_responses.business_description: I cook and sell local food at a small place near the bus stage in Lira. I make posho, beans, rice, matoke and sometimes chicken or fish for the ones who can pay more. I open early morning for the travelers.
intake_responses.customers: Mostly travelers waiting for buses, drivers, and some workers from the nearby shops who come for lunch. They want food that is quick and filling and cheap.
intake_responses.competitors: There are other women cooking food right near me, like three of them. We all sell almost the same food at almost the same price, so it is hard to be different.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I make money from every plate of food I sell. A plate of posho and beans is two thousand, with meat it goes to five thousand. The meat plates give me more profit but fewer people buy them.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest struggle is I never know how much food to cook each day. Some days I cook plenty and it gets wasted by evening, other days I finish early and turn customers away who then go to my neighbours and don't come back. The bus schedules keep changing and I can't predict the crowd.
intake_responses.current_plan: I have started cooking a little less and adding more if the customers keep coming, but this makes some wait too long. I am trying to remember which days are busy but it keeps changing.

intake_responses.business_description: I run a poultry business rearing broiler and layer chickens on the outskirts of Mbarara. I sell eggs to shops and also sell live birds and dressed chicken. I started with two hundred birds and now I have almost eight hundred.
intake_responses.customers: I supply eggs to retail shops and small supermarkets in town, and I sell chicken to restaurants and some households directly. The restaurants are my best customers because they order in bulk.
intake_responses.competitors: There are big farms around Mbarara that produce a lot more than me, and they can sell cheaper because they buy feed in large quantities. I compete more with the medium farmers like myself.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I earn from egg sales daily and from selling birds when they mature. Eggs give me steady income but the feed cost eats a big part of it.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My profit is being killed by the cost of feed, which keeps going up. But here is what confuses me: even when I calculate my egg price to cover the feed, the customers refuse to pay more because the big farms sell cheaper. So I don't know if my feeding is inefficient or if my whole scale is just too small to survive.
intake_responses.current_plan: I am trying to mix my own feed using local maize bran and mukene to cut costs, but I worry the birds are not laying as well. I am also thinking of focusing only on the restaurant contracts.

intake_responses.business_description: I own a small salon in Wandegeya where I do hair plaiting, weaves, manicure and pedicure. I have two other girls who work with me. We mostly serve the university students from Makerere nearby.
intake_responses.customers: My customers are mostly female students and young working women. They like the trendy styles and they always want it done fast because they are busy with lectures and work.
intake_responses.competitors: There are so many salons in Wandegeya, you find like three on the same building. Some are cheaper but their work doesn't last. The students move around comparing prices a lot.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I earn from the different hair services. Plaiting and weaves bring the most money, and I also sell some hair products and extensions to the clients.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My challenge is that my income disappears during the university holidays. When students go home, my salon is almost empty for like two months and I still have to pay rent and the girls. I've tried to attract local women but they don't come as much, and I don't understand if it's my location or my prices that keep them away.
intake_responses.current_plan: During holidays I try to do home service for some clients who call me, and I post my work on WhatsApp status. But it's not enough to cover the slow period so I usually save up during term time.

intake_responses.business_description: I am a wholesaler of household items in Kikuubo, things like basins, plates, jerricans, buckets and plastic containers. I import some from China through agents and buy others locally, then sell to retailers who come from upcountry.
intake_responses.customers: My customers are shopkeepers and market vendors from other towns like Masaka, Mbarara and even from as far as Congo. They buy in bulk to go and resell in their areas.
intake_responses.competitors: Kikuubo is full of wholesalers doing exactly the same thing. Prices are almost the same for everyone so it comes down to who has stock and who gives good credit.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I make a small margin on each item but I sell in large volumes so it adds up. The imported goods give better margin than the local ones.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest headache is that I give my upcountry customers goods on credit and many of them delay paying, sometimes for months. Meanwhile I need cash to restock, so I end up borrowing at high interest. But if I stop giving credit, the customers go to another wholesaler who will. I feel trapped between losing customers and losing my money.
intake_responses.current_plan: I have started keeping a book of who owes me and following up by phone, and I ask new customers for at least half payment upfront. But the old customers resist and I don't want to lose the big buyers.

intake_responses.business_description: I make and sell fresh juice and smoothies from a small stall in Soroti town. I use local fruits like mangoes, passion fruit, pineapple and watermelon. I also sell some snacks like samosas and chapati.
intake_responses.customers: My customers are young people, office workers and students who want something fresh and healthy. Many come in the hot afternoons when they want a cold drink.
intake_responses.competitors: There are soda sellers and other small kiosks selling packaged drinks. Not many people do fresh juice like me in Soroti, so that part I am somehow unique.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I earn from selling the juice cups and bottles, and the snacks bring extra money. A cup of juice goes for two thousand and I make maybe fifty thousand on a good hot day.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My problem is keeping the juice fresh without a good fridge, because the power keeps going off in Soroti. When electricity is gone for hours, my juice spoils and the ice melts, so I lose the stock and customers find warm juice. I don't know if I should invest in a generator or just make smaller batches, but both feel risky with my little capital.
intake_responses.current_plan: For now I make small quantities and only blend when a customer orders, but this makes them wait and some leave. I buy ice from a nearby shop but that also costs me and adds up.

intake_responses.business_description: I run a computer and IT training center in Fort Portal. I teach basic computer skills, Microsoft packages, and some graphic design to students and job seekers. I also do photocopying, printing and internet services on the side.
intake_responses.customers: My customers are secondary school leavers, teachers wanting computer certificates, and civil servants who need the skills for their jobs. The printing side serves anyone who walks in.
intake_responses.competitors: There are two other training centers in Fort Portal and also some people teaching from home cheaply. The printing business has many small players around town too.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I earn from the training course fees which students pay per term, and steady daily income from printing, photocopying and internet browsing.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My challenge is that fewer people are signing up for the full computer courses now, because young people already know how to use phones and think they know computers. But when they get jobs they still lack the real office skills. I can't figure out how to convince them the training is still worth paying for, or whether I should change what I teach completely.
intake_responses.current_plan: I have started offering shorter, cheaper courses focused on specific job skills like Excel for accounts. I am also thinking of adding online marketing training since many now want to sell on social media.

intake_responses.business_description: I buy matoke and other produce from farmers in the villages around Mbale and sell it in bulk at the town market. I also deal in beans and groundnuts sometimes when the season is good. I have been trading produce for over ten years.
intake_responses.customers: My customers are retailers in the market, some restaurants, and traders who transport the matoke to Kampala. The Kampala traders buy the most when they come.
intake_responses.competitors: There are many produce dealers in Mbale doing the same. We all go to the same villages so sometimes we push up the buying price by competing for the farmers.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I make money from the difference between what I buy from farmers and what I sell in the market. Transport and the market dues take a big cut of my profit.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest struggle is the price never stays the same. I buy matoke thinking I will sell higher, but by the time I bring it to market the price has fallen because too much came in that day. Other times prices jump and I have no stock. I can't predict it and I keep guessing wrong, so I don't know if it's the market timing or my sources that are the problem.
intake_responses.current_plan: I try to talk to my fellow traders to know what is coming to the market, and I sometimes hold stock hoping prices rise, but matoke doesn't wait long before it ripens and spoils.

intake_responses.business_description: I do boda-boda transport and small deliveries around Naalya and Kampala. I own my motorcycle now after finishing paying for it. Besides carrying passengers, I do parcel deliveries for online shops and food delivery.
intake_responses.customers: I carry regular passengers who know me, and I get delivery orders through WhatsApp from shops and some restaurants. The delivery jobs pay better and are more reliable than random passengers.
intake_responses.competitors: There are so many boda riders everywhere, and now the app companies like SafeBoda and Bolt have riders too. Passengers prefer the apps because they feel safer and prices are fixed.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I earn from passenger fares and delivery fees. The deliveries give me steady money because the shops call me regularly, while passengers are unpredictable.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My challenge is that fuel prices keep rising but I can't just raise my fares because passengers will refuse and take another boda. The app riders have set prices that customers are used to. I want to shift fully to deliveries which pay better, but I don't have enough regular clients yet to survive on that alone.
intake_responses.current_plan: I am trying to get more delivery contracts by giving my number to shops and being reliable so they call me first. I also joined a savings group with other riders to build capital for maybe a second motorcycle.

intake_responses.business_description: I sell shoes at Gulu Main Market, mostly ladies shoes, sandals and children's shoes. I buy my stock from Kampala, from Owino and Kikuubo, and bring it here to sell. I've had my stall for about four years.
intake_responses.customers: My customers are women buying for themselves and their children, and I sell more during festive seasons and when schools open. The town ladies who work want the nicer heels.
intake_responses.competitors: There are other shoe sellers in the market with similar stock. Sometimes we all bring the same designs from Kampala so customers just pick whoever is cheaper.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I earn from the markup on each pair of shoes. I add maybe five to ten thousand on each pair depending on the type. The children's shoes sell fastest.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My real problem is that my capital is tied up in shoes that don't move. When I go to Kampala I buy what I think will sell, but some designs just sit for months and my money is stuck in them. Then I lack cash to restock the fast-moving sizes. I can't tell if I'm choosing wrong designs or just buying too many of each.
intake_responses.current_plan: I have started buying fewer pairs of each design to test what sells before restocking, but the transport cost to Kampala makes small trips expensive. I sometimes discount the slow shoes to free up cash.

intake_responses.business_description: I sell and install solar systems in Jinja, mostly solar panels, batteries and lighting kits for homes and small businesses. I also do repairs and maintenance for systems I've installed. I have two technicians who help me.
intake_responses.customers: My customers are households in areas with poor grid power, small shops, and some farmers who need power for irrigation pumps or cold storage. Many are in the peri-urban and rural areas around Jinja.
intake_responses.competitors: There are several solar dealers, and also cheap solar products flooding the market that are low quality. Customers can't tell the difference so they often buy the cheap ones that fail.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I earn from selling the solar equipment and from installation fees, plus repeat income from maintenance and repairs. The bigger installations for businesses are more profitable.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My problem is customers want to pay in small installments because the systems are expensive, but my suppliers want full cash upfront when I buy stock. So I'm always short of working capital and can't take on big orders even when customers are ready. Banks want collateral I don't have. I'm not sure if I need a loan, a partner, or a different payment model.
intake_responses.current_plan: I've started asking customers for a deposit before ordering their system, and I sometimes partner with a savings group that lends to my customers so they can pay me directly. But it's slow and I miss opportunities.

intake_responses.business_description: I run a small food joint inside Owino Market where I sell breakfast and lunch to the market vendors and workers. I make katogo, chapati, rolex, tea and full meals at lunch. I start very early in the morning.
intake_responses.customers: My customers are the market vendors, porters and shoppers who don't have time to go home for food. They want quick, affordable and filling meals and they come at the same times every day.
intake_responses.competitors: There are several food sellers in Owino doing similar things. Everyone has their regular customers but we also fight over the new ones and the passing shoppers.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I earn from every meal and cup of tea. Breakfast items like rolex and tea move fast in the morning, and lunch brings the bigger sales with full meals.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My challenge is managing my money because most of my regular customers eat now and promise to pay at the end of the week or month, and many delay or forget. I need daily cash to buy fresh ingredients but it's stuck in these debts. If I refuse credit they'll go elsewhere since they're my loyal base. I don't know how to balance keeping them and staying liquid.
intake_responses.current_plan: I've started writing down who owes me in a notebook and reminding them gently when they come. I try to keep some customers on cash only and give credit only to the most trusted ones.

intake_responses.business_description: I run a fish business in Gulu. I buy fresh and smoked fish, mostly tilapia and Nile perch, from the landing sites and bring it to sell in Gulu market and to restaurants. I've been in this business for about eight years.
intake_responses.customers: My customers are households, restaurants and hotels in Gulu, and some smaller traders who buy from me to sell in nearby trading centers. Restaurants want steady supply.
intake_responses.competitors: There are other fish traders in the market. The fresh fish sellers compete a lot because the fish must sell fast before spoiling, so prices drop in the evening.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I earn from the margin on fresh and smoked fish. Smoked fish keeps longer so I lose less, but fresh fish sells at a better price when it's still fresh.
intake_responses.main_challenge: The distance from the landing sites is my biggest problem. Fresh fish comes far and by the time it reaches Gulu on bad roads, some has already gone bad, especially in hot weather. I lose money on spoilage but if I only sell smoked fish I lose the customers who want fresh. I'm not sure if the answer is better transport, a cold box, or just switching to more smoked fish.
intake_responses.current_plan: I've started using ice boxes for the fresh fish transport and I sell the fresh stock quickly in the morning before selling smoked in the afternoon. But ice and better transport add costs that eat my margin.

intake_responses.business_description: I sell cosmetics and beauty products in Mbarara, things like creams, makeup, perfumes and hair products. I have a small shop and I also sell online through Instagram and WhatsApp. I studied business at university.
intake_responses.customers: My customers are young women, students from the university, and working ladies who care about beauty. The online ones are usually younger and follow beauty trends closely.
intake_responses.competitors: There are many cosmetics shops in Mbarara and also people selling the same products cheaper on social media without a shop, so they have lower costs.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I earn from selling products both in the shop and online. Online is growing but the shop still brings steady walk-in customers who want to test products before buying.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My struggle is deciding how much to invest in the online side versus the physical shop. Online is where young customers are and it's growing, but people order and then don't pay on delivery, or they change their mind. The shop has reliable sales but high rent. I feel like I'm splitting my energy and doing neither one well.
intake_responses.current_plan: I've started asking online customers to pay a deposit through mobile money before I deliver to reduce the cancellations. I'm also posting more videos of the products to build trust with the online buyers.

intake_responses.business_description: I run a carpentry workshop in Jinja making furniture like beds, sofas, tables, chairs and cupboards. I make on order and also keep some ready stock. I have three workers including two apprentices.
intake_responses.customers: My customers are households furnishing their homes, some offices, schools buying desks, and hotels around Jinja. The furnished-home customers are my biggest, especially newlyweds.
intake_responses.competitors: There are many carpenters in Jinja and imported furniture is also coming in cheaply. The imported sofas look nice and some customers prefer them even though mine are stronger.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I earn from selling the furniture and from custom orders which pay better because they're specific. The ready stock helps when customers want something immediately.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest problem is timber. Good hardwood timber has become very expensive and hard to find, and sometimes I buy timber that looks dry but later warps and my furniture bends after the customer takes it. Then they complain and I lose my reputation. I can't tell if I'm buying from bad suppliers or if I need to dry the timber myself before using it.
intake_responses.current_plan: I've started keeping the timber in my workshop for some weeks to dry more before I use it, but this ties up my money and space. I'm also trying to build relationships with two reliable timber dealers.

intake_responses.business_description: I make and supply chapati and mandazi in bulk to shops, schools and small kiosks around Kikuubo and downtown Kampala. I have a small production space and two women who help me make them fresh every morning.
intake_responses.customers: My customers are shopkeepers and kiosks who resell my chapati, some school canteens, and offices that order for their staff. They order in dozens or hundreds daily.
intake_responses.competitors: Many people make chapati but few supply in bulk consistently like me. My competition is other bulk suppliers and shops that decide to make their own instead of buying.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I earn from selling chapati and mandazi in bulk at a wholesale price. I make small profit per piece but the volume is large so it works out.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My challenge is that wheat flour and cooking oil prices keep jumping, but my customers have fixed prices they resell at, so they refuse when I try to raise my price. My margin keeps shrinking and some days I'm almost working for nothing. I don't know if I should reduce the chapati size, find cheaper flour, or find new customers who'll accept higher prices.
intake_responses.current_plan: I've tried buying flour and oil in bulk when prices are low to store, but I don't have much storage or capital to buy a lot. I've slightly reduced the size but I'm scared customers will notice and complain.

intake_responses.business_description: I keep goats and also grow some maize and cassava on my family land near Lira. I sell the goats for meat especially during festive seasons, and I sell the maize and cassava after harvest. I want to grow this into a real farm.
intake_responses.customers: For goats my customers are butchers, restaurants and people buying for celebrations and functions. For the maize and cassava I sell to traders who come to buy from the village.
intake_responses.competitors: Many families around here keep goats and grow the same crops, so when I want to sell, everyone else is also selling at the same time and the buyers push the price down.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I earn a lump sum when I sell goats, mostly during holidays, and I earn from the maize and cassava after each harvest season. It's not steady, it comes in big amounts at certain times.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest problem is that all my income comes in big lumps at harvest and festive times, then for months I have nothing coming in but I still have costs like feeding, school fees and inputs for the next planting. I end up selling my goats cheap when I'm desperate for cash before the good season. I don't know how to spread my income across the year.
intake_responses.current_plan: I'm trying to keep some goats longer to sell during the high-price festive season instead of selling early. I've also started thinking about a small business on the side to bring in weekly cash, but I'm not sure what.

intake_responses.business_description: I run a tailoring business in Gulu making dresses, gomesi, school uniforms and doing alterations. I trained in tailoring and I have two sewing machines and one girl I'm teaching. I make on order mostly.
intake_responses.customers: My customers are women wanting custom dresses and gomesi for functions, parents buying school uniforms, and people who need clothes repaired or resized. Function season brings the most work.
intake_responses.competitors: There are many tailors in Gulu and some work faster or charge less. Ready-made clothes from the mivumba market also compete with me because they're cheaper than custom-made.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I earn from making the garments and from alterations. Custom gomesi and function dresses pay the most, and school uniforms bring steady bulk work when schools open.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My challenge is that when I get a big order like function dresses for a group, I need money upfront to buy all the fabric and thread, but customers only give a small deposit. So I use my own little savings to buy materials, and if the customer delays payment or reduces the order, I'm stuck with materials and no money. I can't tell if I should demand more deposit or stop taking big group orders.
intake_responses.current_plan: I've started asking for at least half the payment before I buy materials for big orders, but some customers refuse and go to another tailor. I keep a little fabric stock for common colors to reduce buying trips.

intake_responses.business_description: I run a hardware shop in Mbarara selling building materials like nails, cement, iron sheets, paint, pipes and tools. I supply both individual builders and some contractors doing projects around the region.
intake_responses.customers: My customers are people building homes, small contractors, plumbers and electricians. The contractors buy in bulk but the individual home builders come more often for smaller amounts.
intake_responses.competitors: There are other hardware shops in Mbarara, some bigger than mine with more variety and better prices from buying in bulk. Customers shop around a lot for cement and iron sheets.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I earn margins on all the items. Cement and iron sheets are high volume but low margin, while paint, tools and fittings give better profit per item.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest struggle is that cement and iron sheet prices from the manufacturers change often, sometimes weekly, and the bigger shops always seem to sell cheaper than my buying price. Customers compare and I lose the sale, but these items bring the traffic that then buys my higher-margin goods. I don't know if I should stop stocking cement or find a way to buy cheaper.
intake_responses.current_plan: I've started buying cement in larger quantities when I have cash to get better prices, and I focus on stocking the fittings and tools the big shops don't bother with. I also give small builders credit to keep them loyal.

intake_responses.business_description: I offer digital services in Mbale, mainly graphic design, social media management for small businesses, and I help people create logos, flyers and manage their online shops. I work from a small office and mostly online.
intake_responses.customers: My customers are small businesses like salons, shops and restaurants that want to look professional online, and some individuals wanting invitation cards or CVs. Most are local Mbale businesses.
intake_responses.competitors: There are a few other designers in Mbale and many online freelancers from Kampala and beyond who charge cheaply. Also, many businesses just use free apps like Canva themselves now.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I earn per design project and monthly fees from the clients whose social media I manage. The monthly social media clients give me steadier income than one-off design jobs.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My challenge is that clients don't understand the value of what I do, so they think design and social media should be very cheap or even free. They pay for one flyer but won't commit to ongoing management even though that's where the real results come from. I struggle to convince small business owners that consistent online presence is worth a monthly fee.
intake_responses.current_plan: I've started showing clients before-and-after results, like how their sales or followers grew after I managed their page, to prove the value. I'm also packaging my services into simple monthly plans so it feels more affordable and clear.

intake_responses.business_description: I sell electronics accessories at Owino, things like phone chargers, earphones, cables, power banks, memory cards and phone covers. I buy stock from importers in Kampala and sell to walk-in customers and some retailers.
intake_responses.customers: My customers are ordinary phone users, students, and small shopkeepers from other areas who buy from me to resell. The retailers buy in bulk while individuals buy one or two items.
intake_responses.competitors: So many people sell the same accessories in Owino and Kikuubo, the prices are almost the same everywhere. It's a very crowded business and margins are thin.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I earn small margins on each item but I sell many. The bulk sales to retailers give steady turnover while walk-ins buy at slightly higher prices.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My real problem is that a lot of my stock is cheap quality and fails quickly, so customers come back angry and I lose them, but the genuine ones are expensive and slow-moving because customers only compare price. I'm caught between selling cheap stuff that damages my name or genuine stuff that doesn't sell. I can't tell if customers actually want quality or just the lowest price.
intake_responses.current_plan: I've started stocking two levels, cheap ones for price-hunters and a few genuine ones for those who ask for quality, and I tell customers the difference. But most still pick the cheap ones and then complain, so it's not fully working.

intake_responses.business_description: I run a small restaurant near Kalerwe market serving local dishes like matoke, rice, posho, beans, meat, fish and greens. I cook fresh daily and serve mostly lunch to workers and traders. I have two people helping me.
intake_responses.customers: My customers are market workers, traders, boda riders and people passing through. They come mostly at lunch time and want a full plate at a fair price, around five to seven thousand.
intake_responses.competitors: There are several eating places around Kalerwe with similar food and prices. Customers move to wherever the food is fresh and the serving is generous that day.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I earn from every plate served at lunch, and I sell some drinks like soda and water alongside. Lunch is my main earner and the meat and fish plates give better margin.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My challenge is that I can't grow beyond my current lunch crowd because my space is small and I only have space and staff for the lunch rush. I want to add supper service or catering for events to earn more, but that needs more staff and money I don't have, and I'm not sure the demand is there in the evening. I feel stuck at the same income level year after year.
intake_responses.current_plan: I've started taking a few catering orders on weekends for small functions to test if that can grow. I'm saving slowly hoping to rent a bigger space, but rent near the market is high and risky.

intake_responses.business_description: I run a small coffee processing and trading business in Fort Portal. I buy coffee cherries and dried coffee from farmers, process it, and sell to exporters and larger buyers. I also help farmers with drying and quality.
intake_responses.customers: My customers are coffee exporters and bulk buyers who want quality processed coffee. I depend on selling in large volumes to these few big buyers who set the standards.
intake_responses.competitors: There are other coffee middlemen and processors in the region buying from the same farmers. The big exporters also sometimes buy directly from farmers, cutting out people like me.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I earn from the margin between buying from farmers and selling to exporters, and better quality processed coffee fetches a higher price than raw cherries.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest struggle is that the coffee price is set by the international market and I have no control over it, so sometimes I buy from farmers at a good price expecting to sell higher, but by the time I've processed it the price has dropped and I make a loss. The farmers also want cash immediately but the exporters pay me later. I can't tell if I should stop guessing prices or find a way to lock in buyers first.
intake_responses.current_plan: I've started trying to agree on a price with an exporter before I buy from farmers so I know my margin, but they're not always willing to commit early. I'm also focusing on better quality since that price is more stable.

intake_responses.business_description: I sell fabrics and materials at Gulu Main Market, including kitenge, gomesi materials, suiting and lining fabrics. Tailors and individuals buy from me to make clothes. I bring my stock from Kampala and Owino.
intake_responses.customers: My customers are tailors who buy for their clients, women buying kitenge and gomesi fabric for functions, and people buying suiting material. Function seasons and holidays are busiest.
intake_responses.competitors: There are other fabric sellers in the market with similar stock, and we often bring the same designs from Kampala. Customers pick whoever has the design they want at the best price.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I earn from the markup on each piece of fabric sold. The kitenge and gomesi materials move well during functions, while suiting is steadier throughout the year.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My challenge is knowing which fabric designs and colors will be in fashion, because trends change fast and if I bring designs that go out of style, they sit on my shelf and my money is locked in them. Meanwhile a new design I didn't stock becomes what everyone wants. I don't know if I should follow trends closely or stick to safe classic materials that always sell slowly.
intake_responses.current_plan: I've started asking the tailors what their clients are requesting so I know what to stock, and I buy small amounts of trendy designs to test before restocking more. I keep classic fabrics as my safe stock that always sells.

intake_responses.business_description: I sell second-hand children's clothes here in Owino, what we call mivumba. I buy in bales from a supplier in Kampala and then sort and sell the pieces one by one to mothers.
intake_responses.customers: Mostly young mothers and grandmothers buying for kids. Some are resellers from smaller towns who come and buy in bulk from me when they visit Kampala.
intake_responses.competitors: There are so many of us in Owino selling the same mivumba, maybe ten stalls in my row alone. We all open the same bales so sometimes we are fighting over the same quality of clothes.
intake_responses.revenue_source: My money comes from the markup on each piece. A good bale can give me maybe 400,000 UGX profit if the sorting is good, but a bad bale can leave me stuck with clothes nobody wants.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My real headache is that I never know what is inside a bale before I pay for it. Sometimes I spend 350,000 on a bale and half of it is torn or stained pieces I can only sell very cheap or throw. The supplier says the bale is grade A but when I open it, it's mixed, and by then my money is already gone.
intake_responses.current_plan: For now I just try to buy from the same supplier so maybe he gives me better bales because he knows me. I also started keeping the torn pieces separate to sell as cleaning rags, but that is small money.

intake_responses.business_description: I run a phone repair shop near Gulu Main Market. I fix screens, charging ports, and I also unlock phones and install software for people.
intake_responses.customers: Young people mostly, students and boda riders whose phones fall and crack. Also some traders in the market who use their phones for mobile money all day.
intake_responses.competitors: There are maybe four other repair guys around here. Some of them charge less than me but they use fake spare parts, so the phone comes back broken after two weeks.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I charge for labour plus the cost of the part. A screen replacement can bring me 30,000 to 50,000 UGX depending on the phone model.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest problem is getting genuine spare parts up here in Gulu. I have to order screens and parts from Kampala, and by the time they reach me the transport and delay has eaten my profit. Sometimes the wrong part comes and the customer has already left angry because I promised the phone in two days and it takes a week.
intake_responses.current_plan: I am trying to keep a small stock of the most common screens like Tecno and itel so I don't wait for Kampala every time. But my capital is small so I can't stock too many models at once.

intake_responses.business_description: I have a small juice bar in Wandegeya near the university. I make fresh juices, smoothies and I also sell fruit salad to students and office people.
intake_responses.customers: University students mostly, and some workers from the nearby offices who want something healthy at lunch. Weekends are slow because students go home.
intake_responses.competitors: There are two other juice places nearby and also the guys selling soda and packaged juice are cheaper than me. Students sometimes just buy a 1000 shilling soda instead of my 5000 shilling smoothie.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I earn from selling each cup of juice or smoothie, and the fruit salad. A good day during the semester I can do 150,000 UGX in sales.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My challenge is that my whole business dies during the university holidays. When students go home for two or three months, my sales drop by more than half but my rent stays the same. I end up eating into my savings just to survive those months, then I struggle to restock when they come back.
intake_responses.current_plan: I am thinking of maybe adding fast food like rolex during holidays to catch the people who stay around. I also want to try delivering to offices but I don't know how to organise that yet.

intake_responses.business_description: I keep dairy cows and sell fresh milk. I have eight cows and I supply milk to some shops and homes in Mbarara town every morning.
intake_responses.customers: Local families who want fresh milk, and two milk shops that buy from me in bulk. Some restaurants also buy when they are making tea for customers.
intake_responses.competitors: There are many dairy farmers around Mbarara because this is cattle country. The big processors like those selling packed milk also compete, but my customers like fresh milk delivered.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I sell milk per litre, around 1200 to 1500 UGX. When the cows are producing well I can get maybe 60 litres a day.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest struggle is that milk goes bad so fast and I have no cold storage. In the dry season my cows produce less but in the wet season they produce plenty and I can't sell it all before it spoils. Sometimes I pour away milk or sell it very cheap to whoever will take it just so it doesn't waste, and that hurts me a lot.
intake_responses.current_plan: I have been trying to find more shops to buy the extra milk in wet season. I also heard about making yoghurt to use the surplus but I don't have the equipment or the knowledge to do it properly.
