intake_responses.business_description: I run a salon on Main Street in Jinja. I do hair plaiting, weaves, nails and also sell some hair products and cosmetics on the side.
intake_responses.customers: Working women, students and some ladies preparing for weddings and functions. Weekends and end of month are my busiest times.
intake_responses.competitors: There are plenty of salons in Jinja, some of them newer and fancier than mine with air conditioning. The younger clients like going where it looks modern even if the work is the same.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I earn from each service, and from the products I sell. Braiding brings the most, maybe 30,000 to 80,000 per client depending on the style.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My real problem is my two workers keep leaving. I train a girl until she is good with clients, then after some months she opens her own small salon nearby and takes my customers with her. So I am always training new people who make mistakes on clients, and the good ones don't stay.
intake_responses.current_plan: Right now I just try to do the important clients myself so they stay loyal to me. I have thought about paying the workers better or giving commission but I am not sure I can afford it with how tight things are.

intake_responses.business_description: I am a wholesaler in Kikuubo. I sell sugar, rice, soap and cooking oil in bulk to smaller shops and retailers who come from villages and other towns.
intake_responses.customers: Shopkeepers from upcountry, small retailers in Kampala, and some restaurant owners who buy sacks of rice and sugar at once.
intake_responses.competitors: Kikuubo is full of wholesalers doing exactly what I do, side by side. We compete mostly on who gives the best price, so our margins are very thin.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I make a small margin on each sack or carton, but because I sell in large volumes it adds up. My turnover is high but the profit per item is very small.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest problem is that many of my retailer customers want to take goods on credit and pay me after they sell. Some pay well but others delay for weeks or disappear, and I have a lot of money sitting out there with people. Meanwhile my own suppliers want cash, so I am squeezed in the middle and sometimes I can't restock even when demand is there.
intake_responses.current_plan: I have started writing down who owes me in a book and following up on phone. I am also trying to only give credit to customers I have known for long, but even some of those have started delaying.

intake_responses.business_description: I do poultry farming in Lira. I keep layers for eggs and I also raise broilers that I sell for meat, mostly around festive seasons.
intake_responses.customers: Egg buyers include shops and some restaurants in Lira town. For the broilers, people buy for parties, weddings and especially at Christmas.
intake_responses.competitors: There are a few other poultry farmers here, and eggs also come from Kampala into the shops which sometimes are cheaper than mine.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I earn steady money from selling eggs by the tray, and bigger lumps when I sell the broilers. A tray of eggs goes for around 11,000 UGX.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest struggle is the cost of feed keeps rising and it is the biggest part of my expenses. When feed prices jump, my egg price can't jump the same way because customers refuse to pay more, so my profit gets crushed. Sometimes I reduce the feed quality to save money but then the birds lay fewer eggs and it's worse.
intake_responses.current_plan: I am trying to mix my own feed using local maize and mukene to cut costs, but I am not sure about the right ratios and my birds' production dropped when I first tried. I am also thinking of buying maize in bulk after harvest when it is cheap.

intake_responses.business_description: I run a small computer training and internet services center in Mbale town. I teach basic computer skills, do printing, photocopying, and help people with online applications like passports and school registrations.
intake_responses.customers: Students, job seekers who need to type CVs, and parents doing online school applications. Also people needing to fill government forms online.
intake_responses.competitors: There are other business centers around town doing printing and photocopy. The training part is where I am a bit different but some schools now teach computers so fewer people pay me for classes.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I earn from training fees, printing per page, photocopy, lamination, and the online service charges. Printing and photocopy bring the daily cash.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest headache is the power in Mbale keeps going off, sometimes for the whole afternoon. When there is no power I can't print, can't run the internet, can't do trainings, and customers just go to the next center that has a generator. I bought a small UPS but it only holds a short time and fuel for a generator eats my profit.
intake_responses.current_plan: For now when power goes I try to send customers to come back later but many don't return. I am saving to buy a solar backup system but it is expensive and I am not sure how much it can actually power.

intake_responses.business_description: I have a small local restaurant in Kalerwe serving matoke, posho, beans, meat and fish to workers and traders in the market area.
intake_responses.customers: Market vendors, boda riders, and porters who want a filling lunch. They come mostly between midday and 3pm.
intake_responses.competitors: There are several food places in Kalerwe like mine, all serving similar local food at similar prices. We compete on portion size and how tasty the food is.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I earn per plate of food, usually 3000 to 5000 UGX depending on what they add. Lunch time is where almost all my money comes from.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My real challenge is judging how much food to cook each day. If I cook plenty and few customers come, the food is left over and by evening it's wasted because I have no fridge. But if I cook little to be safe, I run out during the lunch rush and customers get annoyed and go elsewhere, and I lose sales. I can never get the amount right.
intake_responses.current_plan: I try to remember from the past which days are busy and cook accordingly, but things like rain or when the market is slow mess up my guessing. Sometimes I sell leftover food cheap in the evening to workers going home.

intake_responses.business_description: I do boda-boda transport around Naalya and I also do deliveries for people, like taking parcels and food orders across town.
intake_responses.customers: People needing rides around Naalya and Kampala, and shops or individuals who want things delivered. Some regular customers call me directly.
intake_responses.competitors: There are so many boda riders everywhere, and now the apps like SafeBoda and Bolt bring even more riders competing for the same passengers.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I earn per trip. On a good day I can make 40,000 to 60,000 UGX before fuel, but fuel and the boss's daily payment take a big cut.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest problem is that the boda is not mine, I ride for a boss and I pay him a fixed amount every day whether business is good or bad. On slow days or when it rains and there are no passengers, I still owe him the same money, so I go home with nothing or even in loss. I want my own boda but I can't save because every shilling goes to the daily payment and fuel.
intake_responses.current_plan: I have been trying to build regular customers who call me directly so I get steady trips instead of waiting at the stage. I am also saving small small in a village savings group hoping to one day buy my own machine.

intake_responses.business_description: I sell cosmetics and beauty products in Gulu, things like lotions, makeup, perfumes and hair products. I have a small shop near the main market.
intake_responses.customers: Young women and working ladies who care about their looks, and some men buying gifts. Also a few salon owners who buy products from me to use on clients.
intake_responses.competitors: There are other cosmetics shops in Gulu and also people selling online through WhatsApp and Facebook who don't even have a shop, so they have no rent and can sell cheaper.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I make a margin on each product sold. The imported perfumes and makeup give the best margins but they cost a lot to stock.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My challenge is that customers come to my shop, touch the products, ask questions, then go and buy the same thing cheaper from someone selling on Facebook. I have the rent and stock costs so I can't match those online prices, and I am basically a free showroom for the online sellers. I don't know how to compete when I have costs they don't have.
intake_responses.current_plan: I started my own WhatsApp status posting products but I don't have many followers yet. I am thinking I should also sell online but I am worried about fake orders and how delivery would work here in Gulu.

intake_responses.business_description: I install and repair solar systems in Fort Portal and the villages around. I sell solar panels, batteries, and set up lighting and phone charging systems for homes and small shops.
intake_responses.customers: Rural households without grid power, small shopkeepers, and some schools and clinics. Many are off the main power line so solar is their only option.
intake_responses.competitors: There are cheap solar kits flooding the market, sold in shops without proper installation. People buy those because they are cheaper, then they fail and give solar a bad name.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I earn from selling the equipment plus installation charges. Bigger systems for shops bring good money but those customers are rare.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest problem is that customers judge everything by the upfront price and buy the cheap fake batteries and panels that die in a few months. When those fail, people think all solar is bad, including my quality systems. So I struggle to convince them to pay more for equipment that actually lasts years, because they can't see the long-term value, only today's price.
intake_responses.current_plan: I have started offering a small warranty and telling customers to compare the lifespan, but talk is cheap and they still choose the cheaper option. I want to try a pay-in-installments plan so the quality equipment feels more affordable but I don't have capital to carry that.

intake_responses.business_description: I bake and sell cakes, bread and snacks like samosas and half-cakes in Soroti. I take orders for birthday and wedding cakes and also supply small shops with daily bread.
intake_responses.customers: Families ordering cakes for events, shops that resell my bread and snacks, and walk-in customers who want fresh snacks in the morning.
intake_responses.competitors: There are bigger bakeries in Soroti with machines that produce a lot of bread cheaply, so I can't compete with them on plain bread. But my cakes and custom orders are where I do better.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I earn from the event cakes which are the big orders, and daily from bread and snacks which is smaller but steady.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest struggle is that I mix everything by hand and use a small oven, so I can only make a limited amount each day. When I get a big cake order and also have my daily bread customers, I can't do both well, and I have to turn away orders or deliver late. My capacity is stuck but I feel there is demand I am leaving on the table.
intake_responses.current_plan: I have thought about buying a bigger oven and a mixer but they are expensive and I would need a bigger space too, which means more rent. For now I sometimes wake up very early to try fit everything but I get exhausted and quality suffers.

intake_responses.business_description: I sell shoes in Mbarara Central Market, both new and second-hand. I have men's, women's and children's shoes displayed at my stall.
intake_responses.customers: Regular market shoppers, students needing school shoes, and people passing through the market. Back to school season is very busy for me.
intake_responses.competitors: Many stalls in the market sell shoes, so customers walk around comparing and bargaining hard. Whoever gives the lowest price often wins the sale.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I mark up each pair. School shoes move fast in season, and the second-hand shoes have better margins but I have to sort through them.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My main problem is my capital is tied up in slow-moving sizes and styles. I buy shoes in a range of sizes but the middle sizes sell fast while the very big and very small sizes just sit there for months. So my money is stuck in shoes nobody is buying, and I can't restock the fast-moving sizes because that cash is trapped on the shelf.
intake_responses.current_plan: I sometimes reduce prices on the stuck sizes just to free up money even if I lose. I try to order more of the sizes that sell but the suppliers usually sell in mixed lots so I am forced to take the slow sizes too.

intake_responses.business_description: I am a tailor in Owino Market. I make and repair clothes, do alterations, and I sew school uniforms and simple dresses for customers.
intake_responses.customers: Market traders needing repairs, mothers ordering uniforms, and ladies who bring fabric to have dresses made. Alterations are frequent, uniforms are seasonal.
intake_responses.competitors: There are many tailors in Owino, so there is always someone nearby who can do the same work. Customers go to whoever is free or cheaper.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I charge per garment or per repair. A dress can bring 20,000 to 40,000, repairs are smaller like 2000 to 5000 each.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My challenge is that most of my income is small repair jobs that pay very little, and the big orders like uniforms only come once or twice a year around school opening. I am always busy sewing but not really making good money because the profitable work is seasonal, and the daily repairs barely cover my machine rent and thread.
intake_responses.current_plan: I want to start making ready-made clothes to sell instead of just waiting for customers to bring work, but I need capital to buy fabric upfront and I am not sure what styles will sell. For now I take every small job that comes.

intake_responses.business_description: I do fish farming near Jinja using ponds. I raise tilapia and catfish and sell to restaurants, fish sellers in the market, and some individuals.
intake_responses.customers: Restaurants around Jinja that serve fish, fish vendors in the market, and hotels catering to tourists near the Nile.
intake_responses.competitors: There is a lot of fish coming from Lake Victoria directly which is cheaper, and other fish farmers too. My farmed fish competes with the wild catch on price.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I sell fish by weight when I harvest a pond. A harvest brings a big lump of money but it comes only every few months when the fish mature.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest problem is timing my harvests with the market. When I harvest, sometimes the lake fish are plenty and cheap that week, so I am forced to sell my fish low or hold them longer which costs more feed. I can't easily store the fish, and I can't control when they mature versus when the market price is good. It feels like a gamble every harvest.
intake_responses.current_plan: I have been trying to stagger my ponds so I harvest at different times instead of all at once. I also want to find restaurants who will commit to buying regularly at an agreed price but most want to buy only when they need it.

intake_responses.business_description: I sell household goods and kitchenware online and from a small store in Naalya, things like plates, cookware, storage containers and small appliances.
intake_responses.customers: Mostly women setting up homes, newlyweds, and people who order through my Instagram and WhatsApp for delivery around Kampala.
intake_responses.competitors: There are supermarkets and other online sellers offering the same items. The big supermarkets can order in huge quantities and price lower than me.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I earn a margin on each item. Online orders are growing but delivery costs eat into my profit, and the store brings walk-in sales.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My challenge is managing the online orders and deliveries. Customers order, I send a rider, but sometimes they change their mind at the door, give a wrong location, or don't pick up the phone, and I have paid the rider already. Cash on delivery means I sometimes lose money on failed deliveries, but if I ask for payment upfront many customers refuse because they don't trust online sellers.
intake_responses.current_plan: I have started asking for a small deposit on mobile money before dispatching, but some customers walk away when I ask. I am trying to build reviews and trust on my page so people are comfortable paying first, but it is slow.

intake_responses.business_description: I run a chapati and rolex stand in Mbale town that has grown into a small fast food spot. I sell rolex, chapati, chips, and fried chicken in the evenings.
intake_responses.customers: Students, workers heading home, and young people hanging out in the evening. The evening and night crowd is my main business.
intake_responses.competitors: There are other rolex and chips stands all over Mbale, it's a very common business. Everyone knows how to make rolex so it's easy for anyone to start competing.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I earn per item, rolex around 2000 to 3000, chips and chicken more. Evenings and weekends bring the most cash.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest struggle is that I have three young men working for me at the stand, but I suspect some of the money is not reaching me. The sales feel busy but the cash at the end of the night doesn't match how much we sold. I can't watch the stand every minute, and without a proper way to track what goes out versus what comes in, I don't know if it's theft, waste, or just my bad record keeping.
intake_responses.current_plan: I have started counting the ingredients like eggs and chapati flour at the start and end of the day to estimate sales, but it's rough. I am thinking of being at the stand more myself but I also want to open a second stand which means I can't be everywhere.

intake_responses.business_description: I buy fresh produce like tomatoes, onions, and greens from farmers and sell them in Mbarara Central Market. I sometimes also supply to a couple of restaurants.
intake_responses.customers: Households doing their daily shopping, restaurant cooks, and other small vendors who buy from me to resell in smaller quantities.
intake_responses.competitors: The market is full of produce vendors selling the same tomatoes and onions. When everyone has plenty, prices crash and we all struggle to sell.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I make a margin between the farmgate price and the market price. Fast turnover is key because produce is perishable.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest problem is that tomatoes and greens spoil so quickly, and prices swing wildly. I buy a lot when I get a good farm price, but if the market is flooded that week the price drops and I am stuck with produce rotting on my hands. In a couple of days unsold tomatoes are worthless, so I sometimes sell at a loss just to avoid total waste.
intake_responses.current_plan: I try to buy smaller amounts more often to reduce spoilage risk, but then transport per trip costs me more. I have thought about processing tomatoes into paste or drying them but I don't know how and I fear it won't sell here.

intake_responses.business_description: I sell electronics in Kikuubo, things like phones, radios, speakers, and phone accessories. I import some stock and buy some from bigger importers.
intake_responses.customers: Retailers from upcountry who buy to resell, and walk-in customers looking for a good deal on a phone or speaker.
intake_responses.competitors: Kikuubo has countless electronics dealers, and prices are almost the same everywhere because customers compare quickly. There's also the problem of cheaper stuff coming from other importers undercutting us.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I earn a margin per item. Phones move well but margins are thin because of competition, accessories give better margins.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest headache is the exchange rate. I buy stock in dollars from importers, but by the time I sell in shillings, the dollar has sometimes gone up and my restocking now costs more than what I sold for. So I think I made a profit but when I go to restock I realise I actually can't afford the same quantity. The shilling weakening quietly eats my capital and I only notice too late.
intake_responses.current_plan: I try to sell fast and restock quickly before the rate moves, but that means I can't hold much stock. Some dealers price their goods in dollars but my customers pay in shillings so that's hard for me. I don't really have a good system for this.

intake_responses.business_description: I do catering for events in Gulu, cooking for weddings, funerals, church functions and office meetings. I have a team I call when there is a big function.
intake_responses.customers: Families holding weddings and funerals, churches, NGOs and offices needing catering for workshops and meetings.
intake_responses.competitors: There are a few caterers in Gulu and also some hotels that offer catering. For workshops, the NGOs sometimes have their preferred caterers already.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I charge per plate or a total price for the function. A big wedding can bring good money but I have heavy costs upfront for food and hiring staff.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest challenge is cash flow around functions. Clients want me to cook for 300 people but they pay the full amount only after the event, sometimes weeks later, especially the NGO workshops that pay through slow processes. Meanwhile I have to buy all the food, hire staff, and rent equipment upfront. I often have to borrow expensively or turn down jobs because I can't fund the gap between spending and getting paid.
intake_responses.current_plan: I now try to ask for at least half the payment before the event to buy ingredients, but many clients push back and some competitors don't ask so I risk losing the job. For NGOs I just have to wait and it strains me.

intake_responses.business_description: I build websites and manage social media for small businesses. I work from home and from a co-working spot in Wandegeya, doing digital marketing and simple online stores for clients.
intake_responses.customers: Small shops, restaurants, and startups that want to be online. Some are one-time website jobs, others I manage their pages monthly.
intake_responses.competitors: There are many freelancers and even students doing web and social media cheaply. Also clients sometimes just use free tools themselves once they learn a bit.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I earn from one-off project fees for websites and monthly retainers for managing social media. Retainers are more stable but harder to get.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest struggle is that clients pay me once to build a website or set up their page, then they don't want to pay the monthly fee to maintain it, so my income is very up and down. I finish a project, get money, then have nothing coming in until I hunt for the next client. I want steady monthly income but clients see digital work as a one-time thing, not something ongoing.
intake_responses.current_plan: I am trying to package my services as monthly plans and explain why maintenance matters, but most small clients think once the website exists the job is done. I am also considering focusing on one industry so I get referrals but I haven't decided which.

intake_responses.business_description: I buy matoke and other food from farmers in villages and bring it to sell at Kalerwe market in Kampala. I deal mainly in bananas, and sometimes cassava and yams.
intake_responses.customers: Retailers in Kalerwe who buy bunches to sell in smaller pieces, restaurants, and some households buying whole bunches.
intake_responses.competitors: There are many matoke dealers at Kalerwe bringing truckloads from western and central Uganda. The one who brings good quality matoke at the right time gets the customers.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I make a margin between what I pay farmers and the Kalerwe price, minus the transport which is a big cost.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest problem is the transport and the middlemen at the village. I travel far to buy matoke, but the truck fare keeps rising with fuel, and the village brokers know I've come a long way so they raise their prices on me. By the time I add transport and the broker's cut, my margin at Kalerwe is very thin, and if the matoke arrives bruised from the rough roads I sell it cheaper still.
intake_responses.current_plan: I have been trying to build a direct relationship with a few farmers so I skip the brokers, but they don't always have enough at once. I also share trucks with other traders to split fuel but coordinating everyone is difficult.

intake_responses.business_description: I do metal fabrication in Lira, making window frames, doors, gates, and metal furniture on order. I have a small workshop with welding equipment.
intake_responses.customers: People building homes, shop owners needing security doors and shutters, and some contractors on construction projects.
intake_responses.competitors: There are other welders in Lira, and some customers buy ready-made doors from Kampala or China which come cheaper for standard sizes.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I charge per item made, based on the metal used plus my labour. Big orders like a full house of windows and doors bring good money.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest problem is that the price of metal, especially the tubing and sheets, keeps jumping between when I quote a customer and when I actually buy the materials. I give a price, the customer takes time to decide, and by the time they pay the deposit the metal price has gone up, so I either lose money finishing the job at the old price or I go back and ask for more which annoys the customer and sometimes they cancel.
intake_responses.current_plan: I have started telling customers my quote is only valid for a short time, but they don't like that. I try to buy metal in bulk when prices are low but I don't have much storage or capital to stockpile, so mostly I buy per job.

intake_responses.business_description: I make and sell processed foods in Fort Portal, like packaged groundnut paste, chili sauce, and dried fruit. I supply to supermarkets and shops and also sell at local events.
intake_responses.customers: Supermarkets and shops in Fort Portal and nearby towns, and tourists passing through who like local products as gifts.
intake_responses.competitors: There are bigger processed food brands from Kampala on the shelves that customers already know and trust. Also cheaper unbranded groundnut paste sold loose in the market.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I earn a margin on each packaged product. The supermarket sales are steady but they pay me only after the products sell, and events bring quick cash.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest struggle is getting my products to look professional and trustworthy enough to compete on the supermarket shelf. My packaging and labels look homemade next to the Kampala brands, so customers pick the known brand even though my product tastes better. Proper labels, barcodes, and certification from UNBS cost a lot of money and take time, and without them the good supermarkets don't even want to stock me.
intake_responses.current_plan: I am saving to get proper labels printed and I've started the UNBS certification process but it's slow and expensive. For now I rely on the smaller shops and events where people can taste and know it's local, but that limits how much I can grow.

intake_responses.business_description: I sell second-hand clothes, what we call mivumba, here in Owino. I buy bales from the importers and I open them and sort the clothes for ladies and children. I have been doing this for about six years now.
intake_responses.customers: My customers are mostly women coming to buy for their families, and some small resellers who take from me and go sell in the villages around Kampala. The young people like the good bales with the branded items.
intake_responses.competitors: Eh, there are so many of us selling mivumba in Owino, maybe hundreds on my line alone. Everyone is fighting for the same customer walking past.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I make my money from selling the clothes piece by piece after opening a bale. I take mobile money on MTN and also cash.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My real problem is the bales themselves. When I buy a bale it is closed, I cannot see inside, so sometimes I pay 400,000 shillings and half the clothes inside are torn or old-fashioned that nobody wants. The good ones I sell fast but the bad stock just sits there and I lose money on every bale I open.
intake_responses.current_plan: For now I am trying to buy from one supplier who I think gives better bales, but he is more expensive. I am also thinking maybe I should specialise in only children's clothes because those move faster.

intake_responses.business_description: I run a phone repair shop near Gulu main market. I fix screens, charging ports, batteries, and I also do software flashing when phones hang. I have one boy I am training who helps me.
intake_responses.customers: Mostly young people and boda riders whose phones fall and break. Also business people who need their phones working fast because they use mobile money for everything.
intake_responses.competitors: There are like four other repair guys around here, but honestly the bigger competition is the cheap Chinese phones. When a phone gets a problem people just buy a new cheap one instead of repairing.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I charge for labour and I also sell the spare parts, screens and batteries. Screen replacement is where I make the most money.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest struggle is getting genuine spare parts. The screens I get from Kampala suppliers are sometimes fake copies that fail within two weeks, then the customer comes back angry saying I spoiled their phone. But the original screens cost almost as much as a new phone so customers refuse to pay. I am stuck between cheap parts that ruin my name and expensive parts nobody will buy.
intake_responses.current_plan: I am trying to keep two options, telling customers the price for original and copy so they choose. I also want to travel to Kampala myself to find a trusted parts dealer instead of ordering blindly.

intake_responses.business_description: I have a small juice bar near the central market in Mbarara. I make fresh juice from passion fruit, mango, pineapple and also a mixed one people love. I blend them fresh when the customer orders.
intake_responses.customers: Students from the university nearby, office workers on lunch break, and people who come to the market and want something cold. In the hot months business is very good.
intake_responses.competitors: There are two other juice places but also the sodas and the packaged juices in shops are my competition because they are cheaper and people already know them.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I sell juice by the cup and the bottle. I also do bulk orders for meetings and small parties sometimes.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest problem is the power. When UMEME cuts electricity my blender stops and my fruits in the fridge start going bad. I bought fruits for the whole week but if power goes for two days everything spoils and I throw it away. I cannot afford a generator and even fuel is expensive, so every blackout eats directly into my profit.
intake_responses.current_plan: Right now I buy fruits in smaller amounts more often so less spoils, but that means I pay more per trip to the market. I have been thinking about getting a solar setup but I do not know if it can even run a blender.

intake_responses.business_description: I keep layer chickens for eggs. I have about 400 birds at my place in the outskirts and I bring the eggs to sell at Kalerwe market and to some shops and restaurants around.
intake_responses.customers: I sell mostly to the small dukas and to restaurants that buy trays every day. Some individual customers also come to buy directly because they know my eggs are fresh.
intake_responses.competitors: There are big farms that supply eggs cheaper because they buy feeds in bulk. When their eggs flood the market the price drops and I cannot match them.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I sell eggs by the tray. When the hens finish laying after some time I also sell them as meat birds.
intake_responses.main_challenge: The feed prices are killing me. A bag of layer mash keeps going up but the price of a tray of eggs stays almost the same because of competition. Sometimes I am feeding these birds at a loss just waiting for the egg price to recover, but I cannot stop feeding them or they stop laying. I don't know whether the problem is my feed cost, my flock size, or the market price itself.
intake_responses.current_plan: I am trying to mix my own feed using maize bran and silverfish to cut costs, but I am not sure of the right ratios and my birds' laying dropped a bit. I might reduce the flock to something I can manage cheaper.

intake_responses.business_description: I own a salon on Main Street in Jinja. We do hair braiding, weaves, nails, and I have two girls working with me. We also sell some hair products and creams.
intake_responses.customers: Mostly working women and students. On weekends and before functions like weddings and graduations we get very busy, but weekdays can be quiet.
intake_responses.competitors: So many salons in Jinja now, even someone can just braid from their home and charge less because they have no rent to pay.
intake_responses.revenue_source: We charge for each service, braiding, nails, treatments. I also make small money from selling the hair and products.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest headache is my workers. I trained these two girls from scratch, and once they get good and build their own customers, they leave and open their own small place nearby, and they take my clients with them. So I keep starting over with new trainees who are slow and make mistakes. I feel like I am just training competition for free.
intake_responses.current_plan: I am thinking of giving them commission so they earn more and stay, but that cuts my profit. I also want to focus on being the premium salon with better products so my clients stay loyal to the place, not just the person.

intake_responses.business_description: I sell and install solar systems for homes and small businesses around Naalya and further out where power is not reliable. I do the panels, batteries, and the small home lighting kits.
intake_responses.customers: People in areas where UMEME is bad, some rural customers through referrals, and small shops that want to keep working during blackouts. Also people who want to charge phones and run TVs.
intake_responses.competitors: There are big solar companies with financing plans, and also cheap fake products in the shops that people buy because they are cheaper, then they blame solar when it fails.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I charge for the equipment plus installation. Bigger systems with batteries give me better margins than the small lighting kits.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My problem is that customers want to pay in instalments but I have to buy the equipment upfront in cash. So when a customer says pay me half now and half after two months, I install the whole system but my money is locked up. If they delay the balance, I cannot buy stock for the next customer. I don't have the capital to keep floating everyone yet I lose the sale if I refuse instalments.
intake_responses.current_plan: For now I ask for a bigger deposit before I install, like 70 percent. I am also looking into whether a SACCO or a supplier who gives me stock on credit could help me carry the customers who pay slowly.

intake_responses.business_description: I run a small restaurant in Lira town serving local food, matoke, posho, beans, rice, and meat and chicken. We do lunch mostly and some people come for supper. I cook with two helpers.
intake_responses.customers: Office workers, NGO staff, boda riders, and traders from the market at lunch time. Lunch is my main business, the place fills up between one and two o'clock.
intake_responses.competitors: Many small eating places around, and some new ones opening near the offices. The prices are all almost the same so we compete on taste and speed.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I sell plates of food. Meat and chicken plates cost more so those give me better profit than the plain beans and posho plates.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest struggle is that I cannot predict how many customers will come, so I don't know how much to cook. If I cook plenty and few people come, the food is wasted by evening because I have no fridge big enough and no customers want yesterday's food. But if I cook little and many come, I lose sales and they go to my competitor. Every single day I am gambling on this guess.
intake_responses.current_plan: I am trying to track roughly how many plates I sell each day of the week so I can plan better. I also started making some foods that keep longer, like beans, in bigger amounts and cooking the meat in smaller batches as orders come.

intake_responses.business_description: I have a stall in Kikuubo where I sell phone accessories, chargers, earphones, power banks, phone covers and screen protectors. I buy from the importers there in Kikuubo and sell to smaller shops and individuals.
intake_responses.customers: Retailers from upcountry who come to Kikuubo to stock up, and walk-in customers who need a charger or cover quickly. The upcountry people buy in quantity so they are my best customers.
intake_responses.competitors: Everybody in Kikuubo sells the same things, we are all next to each other selling the same chargers. It becomes about who shouts louder and who gives a slightly better price.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I make money on the margin between the importer price and my selling price. Selling in bulk to upcountry traders is where my volume comes from.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest problem is that customers buy on credit, especially the upcountry traders. They take goods worth two million and promise to pay when they come next time, and some come back, some don't. I have money on the street with people I cannot easily reach because they are in Soroti or Arua. If I refuse credit they buy from the next guy who gives it, but if I give credit I risk not being paid.
intake_responses.current_plan: I am starting to keep a book of who owes what and only giving credit to the ones who have paid me well before. I am also trying to push more mobile money payments so at least there is a record and it is easier to follow up.

intake_responses.business_description: I make and sell chapati and rolex at a small stand in Wandegeya near the university. Morning and evening are my busy times. I have one boy who helps me fry while I take orders and collect money.
intake_responses.customers: Mostly students from Makerere and the hostels around, boda riders, and workers heading home. The students want it cheap and fast, that is the whole business.
intake_responses.competitors: There are rolex stands on almost every corner in Wandegeya. The competition is serious, everyone is right next to each other frying the same thing.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I sell chapati alone and rolex with eggs. The rolex gives more profit than plain chapati because I add the eggs and cabbage.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest challenge now is that the price of wheat flour and cooking oil keeps jumping up, but if I raise my rolex price by even 200 shillings the students complain and go to the next stand. So my costs go up but my selling price is stuck. My profit per rolex keeps shrinking and I can't tell if I should reduce the size, change suppliers, or just accept less money.
intake_responses.current_plan: For now I am buying flour and oil in bigger quantities when the price is a bit down to save something. I am also thinking of adding new items like samosas or a special big rolex that I can charge more for to the customers who have money.

intake_responses.business_description: I do coffee, I buy dried coffee from farmers around Mbale and Bugisu, then I do some processing and sell to bigger buyers and exporters. I also sometimes sell roasted coffee locally in small packs.
intake_responses.customers: My main buyers are the larger coffee dealers and exporters in Kampala who want quantity. Locally I sell small roasted packs to a few shops and hotels.
intake_responses.competitors: Other middlemen buying from the same farmers, and sometimes the big companies send their own agents to buy directly, cutting me out.
intake_responses.revenue_source: Most of my money is from buying coffee cheap from farmers and selling in bulk to exporters at a margin. The local roasted packs are a smaller side income.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest problem is quality control when I buy from many small farmers. Some farmers mix in poorly dried beans or add stones and low grade beans to increase the weight. When I take a big lot to the exporter and they test it and find low quality, they reject it or cut the price heavily, and by then I have already paid the farmers. I lose because I cannot check every single bag properly at the time of buying.
intake_responses.current_plan: I am trying to work with a smaller group of farmers I trust and train them on proper drying. I also want to buy a moisture meter and start grading more carefully before I pay, even if it slows down my buying.

intake_responses.business_description: I sell cosmetics and beauty products, creams, makeup, perfumes and hair products in a shop near Gulu main market. I focus on the quality brands, not the cheap fakes.
intake_responses.customers: Working women, young ladies who care about their skin, and some who buy for reselling in smaller trading centres. Brides and their friends before weddings are good customers too.
intake_responses.competitors: There are other cosmetics shops, plus the ones selling cheap counterfeit products at half my price. Customers sometimes don't understand why mine cost more.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I sell products at retail margin. The imported branded creams and perfumes give me the best profit, and reselling ladies buying in small bulk help my turnover.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest struggle is that a lot of my customers now shop on Instagram and TikTok from sellers in Kampala who post everything online and deliver by bus. My shop is physical, people have to walk in, but the young ladies I depend on are buying online where they see many options with photos. I know I need to sell online too but I don't know how to start, manage the messages, and handle delivery all the way from Gulu.
intake_responses.current_plan: I have started posting some products on my WhatsApp status and I get a few orders. But I struggle to keep up with photographing everything and answering messages while running the shop, so I am not sure how to do it properly without a full time person.

intake_responses.business_description: I have a boda-boda business in Fort Portal. I own three motorcycles, I ride one myself and I have two riders who ride the others and give me a daily amount. We do passengers and also deliveries for shops.
intake_responses.customers: People needing transport around town, students, market women with luggage, and some shops that call us to deliver goods to customers. Deliveries are becoming a good part of the work.
intake_responses.competitors: There are so many boda riders in Fort Portal, and now the SafeBoda and other app riders are coming, so passengers have more choices.
intake_responses.revenue_source: My own riding brings daily cash, and the two riders pay me a fixed daily amount from what they earn on the bikes I own.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest headache is the two riders who use my other motorcycles. They tell me the bike had a problem or business was slow so they pay me less than we agreed, but I can't verify if it's true. And they don't maintain the bikes well, so the machines break down often and the repairs eat my profit. I am not sure if I'm losing money to dishonest riders, to genuine bad business days, or to the bikes just being run down.
intake_responses.current_plan: I am thinking of switching to a system where they slowly buy the bike from me through daily payments, so they take better care of it because it will become theirs. But I worry I might collect all my money and then they leave with a worn-out machine.

intake_responses.business_description: I am a tailor near Amber Court in Jinja. I make dresses, gomesi, kitenge outfits and school uniforms. I sew on order and I also make some ready pieces to sell in the shop.
intake_responses.customers: Women who want custom outfits for functions, families ordering school uniforms in the term season, and walk-ins who want small repairs and adjustments.
intake_responses.competitors: Many tailors in Jinja, and also the ready-made imported clothes that are cheaper than sewing new ones. Some people prefer to just buy finished clothes.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I charge for sewing labour on custom orders and I sell my ready pieces. School uniform orders in bulk during the term opening give me the biggest chunks.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest problem is that my income is very seasonal, it depends on functions and school terms. During school opening and the wedding season I am overwhelmed with work, sometimes turning away customers. But then for months in between it goes very quiet and I struggle to even pay rent and the girl who helps me. The money comes in big waves and then dries up, and I can't smooth it out.
intake_responses.current_plan: In the slow months I try to make ready-made pieces to sell, but they tie up my fabric money and don't always sell fast. I am considering taking on more of the school uniform contracts and maybe teaching tailoring classes during the quiet season for extra income.

intake_responses.business_description: I do fish farming, I have ponds in Soroti where I raise tilapia and catfish. I sell the fish fresh when they mature, mostly to traders and some restaurants and individuals.
intake_responses.customers: Fish traders who buy in bulk to take to the market, local restaurants, and community members who come to buy directly from the ponds when we harvest.
intake_responses.competitors: Fish from Lake Kyoga that traders bring in, which is sometimes cheaper, and other fish farmers around who harvest at the same time and flood the market.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I earn from selling the mature fish by weight at harvest. Catfish and bigger tilapia fetch better prices than the smaller ones.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest struggle is the fish feed cost and the growth rate. Good quality feed is very expensive, but if I use cheap feed the fish grow slowly and stay small, meaning I feed them longer and they fetch less at market. I keep debating whether to spend big on quality feed to grow them fast, or save on cheaper feed but wait many more months. Either way my money is tied up in these ponds for a long time before I see a return.
intake_responses.current_plan: I am experimenting with mixing some quality feed with locally available options and supplementing with things I can grow. I am also trying to stagger my ponds so I don't harvest everything at once and crash the local price myself.

intake_responses.business_description: I sell household goods in Mbale, plates, cups, saucepans, jerricans, buckets, plastic chairs and basins. I have a shop in town and I buy my stock from Kampala and Kenya through Malaba.
intake_responses.customers: Families setting up homes, people buying for weddings and introduction ceremonies, and small retailers from villages who buy a few items to resell.
intake_responses.competitors: Other shops in Mbale selling the same plastics and utensils, and now some supermarkets that stock these things too with fixed lower prices.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I sell at retail margin, and I move more when there are functions in the season. Bulk buyers for weddings give me good single sales.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest problem is the transport and the cost of bringing stock. I bring goods from Kampala and sometimes Kenya, and the transport, loading, and the delays at the border keep going up. By the time my saucepans reach Mbale, the price I must charge is higher than the shops near me who somehow get theirs cheaper. I don't understand if their suppliers are better or they buy in bigger volumes, but my landed cost is killing my competitiveness.
intake_responses.current_plan: I am trying to combine orders with another shopkeeper so we share a truck and reduce transport per item. I also want to find out where exactly the cheaper shops source from because clearly there is a route I am missing.

intake_responses.business_description: I run an IT training and services center in Mbarara. I teach computer basics, packages like Word and Excel, and I also do printing, photocopying, typing and internet services for the public.
intake_responses.customers: Students who need computer skills, job seekers doing CVs and applications, and businesses needing printing and typing. Also people coming to browse or fill online forms.
intake_responses.competitors: Other internet cafes and training centers in Mbarara, and now everyone has smartphones so people do many things on their phones instead of coming to me.
intake_responses.revenue_source: Training course fees are my biggest earner, then printing and photocopying, and small charges for typing and internet use.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest struggle is that the printing and internet side, which used to bring daily cash, is dying because everyone has a smartphone and does things themselves. So I now depend heavily on the training courses, but those come in intakes with gaps between them. My daily walk-in income keeps falling while my rent and internet subscription stay the same every month whether people come or not. I'm not sure whether to invest more in training or find a completely new service to add.
intake_responses.current_plan: I am thinking of adding new courses like graphic design and social media marketing which young people want for jobs. I am also considering offering online services like helping people apply for things and manage their business pages since that is where the demand is going.

intake_responses.business_description: I have a small bakery at Kalerwe where I make bread, buns, and cakes for birthdays and functions. I bake in the morning and supply to shops around, and I take cake orders from customers directly.
intake_responses.customers: Small shops and kiosks that buy my bread and buns to resell, and individual customers who order cakes for birthdays, weddings and parties.
intake_responses.competitors: Big bakeries with brand names whose bread the shops trust, and other small bakers around Kalerwe. The branded bread has a name people already know.
intake_responses.revenue_source: Daily bread and bun sales to the shops give steady income, and the cake orders give bigger one-off amounts with better profit.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest problem is that my bread doesn't stay fresh as long as the branded ones, so shops complain that unsold loaves go hard or moldy in two days and they return them to me or refuse to pay for them. I think it's because I don't use the preservatives the big bakeries use, or maybe my packaging is poor, or my recipe. I keep losing money on returns and I don't know exactly which part of my process is the cause.
intake_responses.current_plan: I have started wrapping the bread better in proper plastic to keep it fresh longer and I am delivering smaller amounts more often so it doesn't sit too long in the shops. I want to learn what the bigger bakeries do to make theirs last.

intake_responses.business_description: I do construction and finishing works, small building projects, tiling, plumbing, and I also make some furniture. I work around Naalya and the suburbs where people are building homes.
intake_responses.customers: People building or renovating their houses, landlords fixing up rentals, and some contractors who subcontract parts of their jobs to me.
intake_responses.competitors: Many small contractors and fundis competing for the same building jobs, and some undercut prices by using cheap materials and cheap labour.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I get paid per project, usually a quote for the labour and sometimes materials too. Bigger finishing jobs like a whole house give better money than small repairs.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest struggle is that I quote a fixed price for a job, but material prices, especially cement, tiles, and iron bars, keep going up in the middle of the project. So by the time I'm halfway, the materials cost more than what I budgeted when I gave the client the quote. The client refuses to add money because we agreed a price, so I finish the job making almost nothing or even a loss. I can't tell if I'm quoting wrong or the market is just too unstable to fix a price.
intake_responses.current_plan: I have started buying most of the materials at the start when I get the deposit, before prices move. I am also trying to write in my agreements that if material prices rise a lot the client shares the difference, but many clients don't like that.

intake_responses.business_description: I grow and sell groundnuts and simsim. I have a garden where I grow them, and I also buy from other farmers, then I sell in the Gulu market both raw and as ground paste, what we call odii.
intake_responses.customers: Market women who buy the paste for cooking, households, and some traders who take the groundnuts to Kampala. The odii paste sells well because people use it for local dishes.
intake_responses.competitors: Many women in Gulu market selling the same groundnuts and simsim, and traders from other districts bringing theirs when prices there are low.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I sell raw groundnuts and simsim by the basin, and I make more profit from the ground paste because I add value by processing it.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest problem is storage and the aflatoxin issue. When I keep the groundnuts to wait for a better price, some get moldy and develop that poison, and buyers who know refuse them, or I have to sell cheap. But if I sell immediately at harvest the price is very low because everyone is selling at the same time. I'm caught between selling cheap now or risking my stock spoiling while I wait, and I don't have a proper dry store.
intake_responses.current_plan: I am trying to dry them very well in the sun before storing and keeping them off the ground on tarpaulins. I want to save enough to build a small proper store so I can hold my stock safely until prices are good after the season.

intake_responses.business_description: I sell shoes in Kikuubo, mostly men's shoes, sneakers and official shoes. I buy from importers and sell to retailers who come from upcountry and also to individual walk-in customers.
intake_responses.customers: Retailers from towns like Masaka, Mbarara and Hoima who come to Kikuubo to stock shoes, and individual customers looking for a good deal on shoes.
intake_responses.competitors: So many shoe sellers in Kikuubo all in the same building selling similar stock. It's a price war, whoever offers cheaper wins the retailer that day.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I make my margin between the importer price and my selling price. Bulk sales to upcountry retailers move my stock fastest.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest struggle is choosing which shoes to stock. I put my capital into what I think will sell, like a certain style or colour, but sometimes fashion changes and those shoes just sit there while a different style is what everyone suddenly wants. My money gets stuck in dead stock I have to sell at a loss later, and I don't have a good way to predict what will move before I commit my capital.
intake_responses.current_plan: I am trying to buy smaller quantities of new styles first to test if they sell before I buy plenty. I am also asking my upcountry retailers what their customers are asking for so I stock based on real demand rather than guessing.

intake_responses.business_description: I run a catering and events business from Wandegeya. I cook for weddings, introductions, office parties and meetings, and I hire out tents, chairs, and decorations. I bring in casual staff when I have big functions.
intake_responses.customers: Families planning weddings and introductions, offices and NGOs doing events and workshops, and churches with functions. Weekend functions are the bulk of my work.
intake_responses.competitors: Many catering companies in Kampala, some bigger and more established with better equipment and vans, competing for the same wedding and corporate clients.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I charge per plate for catering plus rental fees for the tents, chairs and decor. Big weddings and corporate contracts bring the most money at once.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest challenge is managing several functions on the same weekend with the same limited equipment and staff. Sometimes I get two weddings on one Saturday and I only have enough chairs and tents for one, so I either turn down business or rush to rent more from others which eats my profit. But I can't buy more equipment for peak days because it would just sit idle on the slow weekends. I don't know how to size my capacity right.
intake_responses.current_plan: I have built relationships with other suppliers so I can sub-rent equipment when I'm overbooked, sharing the profit. I am also thinking of specialising more in the catering side, where I make good margins, and partnering with a dedicated tent company rather than owning everything myself.

intake_responses.business_description: I run a maize milling business in Lira. Farmers bring their maize and I mill it into flour for a fee, and I also buy maize, mill it, and sell the posho flour in bulk to shops and schools.
intake_responses.customers: Local farmers who come to mill their own maize, shops buying flour to resell, and schools and institutions that buy posho in bulk for feeding.
intake_responses.competitors: Other millers in Lira with bigger and faster machines, and traders bringing cheaper milled flour from other areas during good harvest seasons.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I charge a milling fee per bag for farmers, and I profit on the flour I buy, mill, and sell to shops and schools.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest problem is that my old milling machine keeps breaking down, and when it's down I lose customers who just go to the next miller and often don't come back. The repairs are expensive and the spare parts sometimes take days to come from Kampala. I know I need a better machine, but a new one costs a lot and I can't get a loan easily, so I keep patching this old one and losing business every time it fails.
intake_responses.current_plan: I am saving up slowly and pricing spare parts for a bigger machine. I am also looking into whether a group of us millers or a SACCO could help me access financing, because the bank wants collateral and interest that I cannot manage right now.

intake_responses.business_description: I make and sell yoghurt and some dairy products in Fort Portal. I buy fresh milk from farmers around, process it into flavoured yoghurt, and sell it in bottles to shops, schools and directly to customers.
intake_responses.customers: Shops and kiosks that stock my yoghurt, schools buying for children, and individual customers who like the flavoured yoghurt. Children and young people are my biggest fans.
intake_responses.competitors: Bigger dairy brands from Mbarara and Kampala that have their yoghurt in every supermarket already, plus a couple of other local yoghurt makers here.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I sell yoghurt by the bottle, retail to customers and at a lower price in bulk to shops. Selling directly gives more profit per bottle than through shops.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest struggle is the cold chain. My yoghurt needs to stay refrigerated but many of the small shops I supply don't have reliable fridges, or power goes off, so my yoghurt spoils on their shelves before it sells. Then they blame me and return the spoiled ones, and my brand gets a bad name for going bad quickly, even though the real problem is their storage. I can't afford to give every shop a fridge.
intake_responses.current_plan: I am now focusing more on shops that actually have working fridges and generators, and delivering smaller amounts frequently so it doesn't sit long. I'm also thinking of getting a cooler box and doing more direct sales to customers myself to control the freshness.

intake_responses.business_description: I own a hardware shop in Soroti selling building materials, nails, iron sheets, cement, paint, pipes and tools. People building homes and small contractors are my main market. I've run it for over ten years.
intake_responses.customers: People building or renovating houses, small contractors and fundis buying materials for jobs, and farmers buying iron sheets and pipes for their needs.
intake_responses.competitors: A few other hardware shops in Soroti, and some customers now buy directly from Kampala or Mbale suppliers in bulk to save money, cutting out shops like mine.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I sell materials at retail margin. Cement and iron sheets move in volume, and paint and smaller items give better margins per item.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest problem is that a lot of my capital is tied up in slow-moving stock like certain pipe sizes, paint colours, and tools that customers rarely ask for, while the fast movers like cement and common iron sheets I sometimes run out of because my money is locked in the slow stuff. My shop looks full but my cash is frozen on the shelves, and I struggle to restock the things that actually sell fast.
intake_responses.current_plan: I am trying to clear the slow stock with discounts to free up cash, even if I lose a little. I want to keep a closer eye on what sells fast and reorder those quickly, and only stock small amounts of the rare items when someone specifically orders them.

intake_responses.business_description: I run a mushroom growing business in Naalya. I grow oyster mushrooms in a small shaded structure and sell them fresh and also dried. I've been building it up over the last three years.
intake_responses.customers: Health-conscious people, some supermarkets and grocery shops, restaurants that put mushrooms on their menu, and individual customers who order through my WhatsApp.
intake_responses.competitors: A few other mushroom growers in Kampala, and imported dried mushrooms. Fresh mushrooms are not something everyone eats yet, so the market is still small.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I sell fresh mushrooms by weight, which is my main income, and dried ones which last longer and I can sell over time and at a higher price per kilo.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest challenge is that demand is still small and inconsistent, so I sometimes harvest more fresh mushrooms than I can sell before they spoil in two or three days. I have to rush to dry the excess but drying reduces the value and takes effort. The real issue is the market itself, many Ugandans still don't know how to cook or value mushrooms, so I'm limited by low awareness rather than my ability to grow them.
intake_responses.current_plan: I have started sharing recipes and cooking ideas on my WhatsApp and Instagram to teach people how to use mushrooms and grow the demand. I am also trying to sign up more restaurants and hotels as regular buyers so I have steady orders to plan my growing around.

intake_responses.business_description: I sell second-hand clothes, what we call mivumba, at Owino. I buy the bales from the importers in Kampala and I sort them out myself before I hang them up. Mostly I do ladies' dresses and children's clothes.
intake_responses.customers: My customers are ordinary women, especially those coming to buy for their families before school opens. Some are retailers from upcountry who come and buy in small quantities to resell in their villages.
intake_responses.competitors: Eh, the competition is too much. In just my line there are maybe twenty people selling the same mivumba, and when one opens a bale everybody rushes to buy the same style so we all end up with the same things.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I make my money from selling the clothes piece by piece. On a good day like Saturday I can move plenty, but weekdays are slow.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest struggle is that when I open a bale I never know what quality is inside. Sometimes I pay 300,000 for a bale expecting good grade-one clothes but half of them are torn or faded, so I lose. The importer won't refund me and I can't open before buying, so it's like gambling every week.
intake_responses.current_plan: I am trying to build a relationship with one importer who I trust so maybe he gives me better bales. I also started keeping the torn ones and selling them cheap to tailors instead of throwing them away.

intake_responses.business_description: I run a phone repair shop near Gulu Main Market. I fix screens, batteries, charging ports, and I also do software flashing for phones that hang. I have been doing this for about six years now.
intake_responses.customers: Mostly young people, students and boda riders whose phones fall and crack. Some business people also bring their phones when they get water damage or the screen goes black.
intake_responses.competitors: There are other repair guys around, maybe five or six shops close to me. Some of them charge very low prices even when their work is poor, so customers go to them first and only come to me after their phone gets spoiled again.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I earn from the repair labour and from selling the spare parts like screens and batteries. I also make small money selling phone accessories, chargers, pouches, screen guards.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest problem is getting genuine spare parts. The screens I get from the Kampala suppliers are sometimes fake copies, so I fit them and within two months the customer comes back complaining. Then they blame my work, not the part, and I have to redo it for free which eats my profit. I can't tell the fake from the real one until it fails.
intake_responses.current_plan: I have started buying parts only from two suppliers who give me a small warranty, but their prices are higher so I struggle to compete on price. I am thinking of telling customers upfront about original versus copy so they choose.

intake_responses.business_description: I make and sell fresh fruit juice, mostly passion, mango and watermelon, from a small stall in Kalerwe. I blend it fresh and sell in bottles. I started after I finished my degree and couldn't find a job.
intake_responses.customers: Office workers passing by in the morning, gym people, and mothers who buy for their children. On hot days I sell a lot, but when it rains the customers just disappear.
intake_responses.competitors: There are the packaged juices in the shops like Splash and the cheap ones, and also two other ladies selling fresh juice near me. Some customers think the packaged ones are safer even though mine is natural with no additives.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I earn from selling the bottled juice, and sometimes I get orders for meetings and small parties where I supply in bulk.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest challenge is that the fruit prices jump up and down so much I can't set a stable price. In dry season a box of passion fruit doubles, but customers refuse when I raise my price, so I either sell at a loss or reduce the quantity in the bottle, and then they complain the bottle got smaller. I feel stuck between the farmers and the customers.
intake_responses.current_plan: I am trying to buy fruit directly from farmers in Mpigi to skip the middlemen, but transport is a problem for small amounts. I also want to start freezing pulp when fruit is cheap so I have stock for the expensive months.

intake_responses.business_description: I keep layer chickens for eggs. I have about 800 birds now on my land just outside Mbarara town, and I supply eggs to shops and kiosks in the central market. I started with 100 birds five years ago.
intake_responses.customers: My main customers are shopkeepers and a few restaurants who buy trays every week. Some individual families also come directly to my farm because they know my eggs are fresh.
intake_responses.competitors: There are bigger farms that supply supermarkets and can sell cheaper because they buy feed in tonnes. There are also eggs coming from other districts that flood the market and push the price down.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I earn from selling eggs by the tray, and when the layers get old I sell them off as meat birds to get some lump sum money back.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest problem is that feed is now more than half of all my costs and the price keeps climbing, but the egg price at the market stays the same or even drops when there's oversupply. So my margin is being squeezed from both sides. Some months I'm basically working just to feed the chickens and not making real profit.
intake_responses.current_plan: I am experimenting with mixing my own feed using local maize bran and mukene to cut the cost, but I'm worried it might reduce how many eggs they lay. I'm also thinking of finding contract buyers who guarantee a price.

intake_responses.business_description: I have a small local restaurant, what we call a kibanda, near Main Street in Jinja. I cook matoke, posho, rice, beans, meat and greens for lunch. I open around ten and by three the food is usually finished.
intake_responses.customers: My customers are workers from the nearby shops, boda riders, and market people who want a cheap filling lunch. Most of them come at the same time between one and two o'clock.
intake_responses.competitors: There are many other kibandas around, maybe seven on my street alone. We all sell almost the same food at almost the same price, so customers just go to whoever is nearest or whose food they liked last time.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I make money from selling plates of food at lunch. I charge more if someone wants meat and less for just beans and posho.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest struggle is that I can't predict how many customers will come, so I either cook too much and it spoils by evening since I have no fridge, or I cook too little and customers turn away when the food finishes early. Either way I lose. When I throw away food that's my capital gone, but when I run out I lose the customer to my neighbour.
intake_responses.current_plan: I have started asking my regular customers in the morning if they will come for lunch so I can guess the numbers. I also want to save up for a fridge so leftover food can be kept and sold the next morning.

intake_responses.business_description: I import and wholesale household goods, things like plastic basins, buckets, jerrycans and thermos flasks, from a shop in Kikuubo. I sell mostly in bulk to retailers who come from all over the country.
intake_responses.customers: My customers are retail shopkeepers from upcountry towns like Masaka, Fort Portal and even South Sudan traders. They buy in cartons and dozens to go and resell.
intake_responses.competitors: Kikuubo is full of people selling the exact same Chinese plastics. When a new container lands, prices crash because everybody wants to sell first, so we undercut each other until nobody makes good money.
intake_responses.revenue_source: My revenue is from the markup on the goods I sell in bulk. I make small margins but move large volumes, so it depends on turnover.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest problem is that a lot of my customers buy on credit and pay when they've sold. When I trust them and give goods on credit, my cash gets tied up and I can't order the next container in time, but if I refuse credit they just go to my competitor who gives it. So I'm forced to finance my customers' businesses with my own money, and when one disappears without paying I take a big hit.
intake_responses.current_plan: I have started keeping a book of who owes what and setting limits, but enforcing it is hard because these are old customers. I'm thinking of asking for at least half payment upfront on new orders.

intake_responses.business_description: I run a hair salon in Gulu where I do braiding, weaves, relaxing and nails. I trained at a vocational school and rented a small space with two chairs. I have one girl who helps me on busy days.
intake_responses.customers: Mostly young women and working ladies who come for their hair before functions and month-end. Students come during holidays when they have some money from home.
intake_responses.competitors: There are salons everywhere in Gulu now, and some new ones opened right near me with fancy decoration and lower prices to attract customers. Some ladies also just do hair at home for their friends very cheaply.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I earn from the hair services, and I also sell the hair extensions and products like sprays and gels to the customers who come.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest challenge is that my income is completely uneven across the month. Around month-end and before big functions I'm so full I turn people away, but in the middle of the month I can sit two days without a single customer. Because of that I can't plan, I can't pay my helper steadily, and I end up borrowing during the slow days then repaying at month-end, which never lets me grow savings.
intake_responses.current_plan: I am trying to introduce cheaper simple styles during the slow weeks to keep some money coming in. I also started a small WhatsApp group to remind customers and post my work so they book in advance.

intake_responses.business_description: I run a small IT and computer training centre in Lira. I teach basic computer skills, Microsoft packages, and internet use, and I also offer printing, photocopying and typing services on the side.
intake_responses.customers: Mostly students who want computer certificates, job seekers who need to type applications, and NGO workers who come to print reports. Some parents bring their children during holidays for lessons.
intake_responses.competitors: There are two other training centres in town, and now many young people have smartphones so they think they don't need to learn computers. The internet cafes are also dying because everyone browses on their phone now.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I earn from the training course fees which people pay in installments, and from the daily printing and photocopy work which brings steady small cash.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest struggle is that the training side and the printing side pull me in two directions. The printing brings small daily cash that keeps the lights on, but it distracts me from teaching, and when I'm teaching the printing customers leave because nobody serves them. I can't afford another staff yet, so I'm losing income on whichever side I'm not attending to, and neither one grows properly.
intake_responses.current_plan: I'm thinking of training one of my former students to handle printing so I focus on teaching, and pay them a commission instead of a fixed salary. I also want to add online-focused courses like data entry since that's where the demand is going.

intake_responses.business_description: I sell shoes in Mbale town, both new and slightly used, mostly for women and children. I display them outside my small shop and I also carry some to sell at village markets on market days.
intake_responses.customers: Women buying for themselves and their children, especially before school opens and during festive seasons. Some men come for the church and office shoes I keep in a small selection.
intake_responses.competitors: There are many shoe sellers in the town center and along the road, and the ones in the arcade have more variety. The Chinese shops also bring very cheap plastic shoes that undercut my leather ones.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I earn from selling the shoes with a markup, and I make a bit more on the village market days because there's less competition there.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest problem is that fashions and sizes change fast, and I keep guessing wrong on what to stock. I buy a lot of one style thinking it will move, and then it sits for months while customers ask for something else, so my money gets locked in shoes nobody wants. Meanwhile I don't have cash to buy the styles that are actually selling. It's like I'm always one step behind what customers want.
intake_responses.current_plan: I've started buying smaller quantities of many styles instead of many of one, to test what sells before committing. I'm also noting down what customers ask for that I don't have, so I stop guessing.

intake_responses.business_description: I do boda-boda transport and I also own two other bikes that I gave to riders on a hire agreement where they pay me daily and eventually own the bike. I operate around Wandegeya and the university area.
intake_responses.customers: Students, office people going to work, and I do a lot of deliveries now, taking food and parcels for people who order on their phones. Weekends are good because of the nightlife around here.
intake_responses.competitors: There are too many boda riders now, and the app companies like SafeBoda and Bolt brought in even more riders who accept low fares. Customers now compare prices on the app so they don't want to pay my normal fare on the street.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I earn from the rides and deliveries I do myself, plus the daily payments from the two riders using my other bikes.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest challenge is the two bikes I hired out. One rider pays well and takes care of the bike, but the other one is always behind on payment and the bike keeps breaking because he rides it carelessly. When it breaks I pay for repairs but he still doesn't pay the daily fee, so that bike is actually costing me money instead of earning.
