I don't know if I should take it back or keep hoping he improves.
intake_responses.current_plan: I have started writing down the daily payments so I can see clearly who is paying and who is not. I'm considering putting a written agreement with penalties, and maybe finding a more serious rider for that second bike.

intake_responses.business_description: I run a small bakery from home in Naalya making cakes, cupcakes and cookies mostly for birthdays, weddings and office events. I take orders on Instagram and WhatsApp and deliver around Kampala.
intake_responses.customers: Young families celebrating birthdays, couples planning weddings, and companies ordering for staff events. Most of them find me through Instagram and referrals from happy customers.
intake_responses.competitors: There are so many home bakers now on Instagram, all posting nice cakes. Some charge very low prices that I can't match, and the established bakery shops in town have physical locations that make customers trust them more.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I earn per cake order, with wedding cakes bringing the most money. I also sell boxes of cookies and cupcakes for smaller everyday orders.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest struggle is that almost all my orders are for weekends, so Saturday I'm overwhelmed doing five cakes at once with one oven, but Monday to Thursday my oven sits cold and I earn nothing. I turn away weekend orders because I can't physically make them all, so I'm losing money I could have earned, but I can't fill the weekdays because nobody wants cake on a Tuesday. My capacity and my demand just don't match up.
intake_responses.current_plan: I'm thinking of pre-baking and freezing some cake layers earlier in the week so I can decorate faster on weekends and take more orders. I also want to push weekday products like bread and packed snacks to offices to fill the empty days.

intake_responses.business_description: I grow and sell Irish potatoes on rented land around Fort Portal, and I also buy from other small farmers to bulk up and sell to traders coming from Kampala. I've been in this for about eight years.
intake_responses.customers: My main buyers are traders who come with trucks from Kampala and Mbarara to buy in bulk, and some restaurants and chip sellers who come directly for smaller quantities.
intake_responses.competitors: Every farmer here grows Irish potatoes, so at harvest time everyone is selling at once and the traders know it. They come and offer very low prices because they know we're desperate to sell before the potatoes rot.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I earn from selling my own harvest and from the margin on the potatoes I buy from other farmers and resell in bigger volumes.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest problem is timing the sale. When I harvest, everyone else harvests too, so the price is on the floor and the Kampala traders squeeze us. But if I wait for the price to rise, my potatoes start rotting in storage because I don't have a proper cold store, so I'm forced to sell cheap anyway. The buyers hold all the power because they know my potatoes are perishing.
intake_responses.current_plan: I'm looking into building a simple ventilated store to keep potatoes longer so I can sell when prices are better. I'm also trying to form a group with other farmers so we can sell together and negotiate stronger prices with the traders.

intake_responses.business_description: I sell mobile phone accessories and do mobile money in Soroti town, a small stall with chargers, earphones, phone covers, memory cards and both MTN and Airtel float. I've been running it for three years.
intake_responses.customers: All kinds of people, mostly for mobile money since everyone sends and receives money here. The accessories sell to young people and anyone whose charger has spoiled.
intake_responses.competitors: There are mobile money agents at almost every corner now, so people just go to whoever is nearest. For accessories, the same cheap items are everywhere, so there's nothing special about mine.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I earn commission on the mobile money transactions and profit on the accessories I sell. The mobile money brings the most steady income.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest struggle is managing my float for mobile money. When many people want to withdraw cash, I run out of cash and have to send them away; when many want to deposit, I run out of e-value on my line. I keep having to rush to the bank or a super-agent to rebalance, and sometimes I miss customers during that time. On top of that, keeping large cash at the stall makes me a target for thieves. Balancing the two sides eats my whole day.
intake_responses.current_plan: I'm trying to learn the daily patterns, like withdrawals are high in the morning and deposits in evening, so I keep the right balance. I'm also thinking of getting a second SIM float and keeping less cash by banking more often.

intake_responses.business_description: I do fish farming with earthen ponds outside Mbale, mostly tilapia and some catfish. When they mature I harvest and sell to markets and to women who fry and sell fish. I have four ponds now.
intake_responses.customers: Fish traders and market women who buy to resell, and some restaurants and hotels in Mbale that want fresh fish. During events people come directly to buy for their functions.
intake_responses.competitors: There's fish coming from Lake Victoria and the big lakes that is cheaper because they catch it wild. Some other farmers around here also sell, and the imported frozen fish in supermarkets competes on price.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I earn from selling the mature fish by weight at harvest. It comes in big lump sums a few times a year when a pond is ready.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest problem is the long wait with no income in between. The fish take six to eight months to mature, and during all that time I'm spending on feed and pond maintenance with zero money coming back. By harvest I've often had to borrow to keep feeding them, and then a big chunk of the harvest money goes to repaying debts, so I never build up capital to expand. The gap between spending and earning is killing me.
intake_responses.current_plan: I'm trying to stagger my ponds so they don't all mature at the same time, giving me some income throughout the year instead of all at once. I'm also looking at growing catfish which matures a bit faster to shorten the waiting.

intake_responses.business_description: I'm a tailor in Owino, I make and repair clothes, do alterations, and I sew school uniforms and simple dresses on order. I have one sewing machine and an overlock that I share with another tailor.
intake_responses.customers: Market people who need quick repairs, mothers ordering school uniforms, and ladies who bring their own material for me to sew into dresses and gomesi for functions.
intake_responses.competitors: There are many tailors in Owino, some more experienced than me with better machines. The ready-made imported clothes are also so cheap now that people prefer buying finished than paying me to sew.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I earn per garment I sew and per repair job. The school uniform season brings a lot of work in bulk when schools are opening.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest challenge is that customers bring their material and want the dress finished by a certain date, but I often promise too many people the same deadline and then can't finish them all with just one machine. When I delay, they get angry and some take their material back, and word spreads that I'm slow. But if I refuse work I lose the income. I keep overcommitting because I fear turning away customers, and it's hurting my name.
intake_responses.current_plan: I'm trying to be honest about realistic dates instead of just saying tomorrow to please everyone. I'm also saving to buy my own overlock machine so I stop waiting to share and can work faster.

intake_responses.business_description: I sell and install solar systems in Mbarara, small home kits with panels, batteries and lights, plus solar for pumping water. I do the sales, delivery and installation myself with one technician.
intake_responses.customers: Mostly rural families off the grid, small farmers who want to pump water, and shops in trading centres without reliable power. Some schools and clinics also buy from me.
intake_responses.competitors: There are cheap solar products flooding in from town, some are fake with batteries that die in months. Customers who got burned by fakes now don't trust solar at all, and there are also other dealers with lower prices.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I earn from selling the systems and from the installation service. I also make some money replacing batteries and repairing systems people bought elsewhere.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest struggle is that my good quality systems cost more, but customers only compare the upfront price and choose the cheap fake ones from the next shop. Then those fail in a year and the customer curses all solar, including mine. I know my products last longer and are cheaper over time, but I can't get customers to see beyond the sticker price, and I can't drop my price to match junk. So the market is being spoiled by fakes and it drags me down with it.
intake_responses.current_plan: I'm starting to offer a written warranty and let customers pay in installments so the higher quality feels affordable. I'm also trying to show past customers' working systems as proof that quality lasts.

intake_responses.business_description: I make and sell chapati and rolex at a roadside stand near Gulu Main Market. I start in the evening and sell into the night. I have two helpers who fry while I take orders and money.
intake_responses.customers: Students, boda riders, night workers and people passing by hungry in the evening. On weekends the young people buying after drinking are my best customers.
intake_responses.competitors: There are chapati stands all along the road, we're almost next to each other. We all sell rolex at nearly the same price, so it comes down to whose chapati is softer and who serves faster.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I earn per chapati and per rolex sold. Selling the rolex with eggs and cabbage inside brings more profit than plain chapati.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest problem is that my costs for flour and cooking oil have gone up so much, but if I raise my rolex price even by 200 shillings, customers complain loudly and go to the next stand. So I've kept the same price for over a year while my ingredients cost more and more, and my profit per rolex has shrunk to almost nothing. I'm working harder and selling the same amount but taking home less. I feel trapped by the price everyone expects.
intake_responses.current_plan: I'm thinking of introducing a bigger 'special' rolex with more fillings at a higher price so customers who can pay more have an option, while keeping the standard one. I'm also buying flour and oil in bulk to get a better price.

intake_responses.business_description: I run a small metal fabrication workshop making window frames, doors, gates and burglar-proofing for buildings. I have three workers and we work on order for people who are building homes.
intake_responses.customers: People constructing houses, contractors doing small projects, and shop owners who want metal shutters and displays. Most come through referrals from people I've worked for before.
intake_responses.competitors: There are many welders around, some cheaper because they use thinner metal and cut corners. Customers often just take the lowest quote without understanding the quality difference in the metal gauge.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I earn from each fabrication contract, charging for materials plus labour. Big projects like a full house of windows and doors bring good money at once.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest struggle is with power. The load shedding here is unpredictable, and my welding and cutting all need electricity, so when power goes I sit idle with workers I'm still paying. Sometimes it's off for hours and I miss delivery deadlines, then customers think I'm unreliable. I bought a small generator but the fuel cost eats my profit, so running it makes some jobs actually lose money. I'm caught between missing deadlines or losing profit to fuel.
intake_responses.current_plan: I'm trying to schedule the heavy cutting work for the hours power is usually stable, and use the generator only for urgent finishing. I'm also thinking of investing in a bigger, more fuel-efficient generator if I can raise the capital.

intake_responses.business_description: I sell women's clothing and accessories online, dresses, bags and shoes that I source from Kampala and sometimes order from Dubai and Turkey through agents. I post everything on Instagram and TikTok and deliver.
intake_responses.customers: Working-class young women in Kampala who like trendy fashion and shop from their phones. Many are busy professionals who don't have time to go to markets.
intake_responses.competitors: There are hundreds of online fashion vendors now, all posting similar imported clothes. Some sell cheaper because they order fakes or lower quality, and the big established boutiques have loyal followings.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I earn from the markup on each item I sell, and delivery I charge separately. My best months are festive seasons and December when people buy for parties.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest problem is customers who order and then refuse to pick up or pay on delivery. They message excitedly, I package it and pay the delivery rider upfront, then the customer goes silent or claims they changed their mind when the rider arrives. So I lose the delivery fee and the item comes back, sometimes handled and no longer new. This happens so often it's eating my profit, but if I demand full payment before delivery, many customers don't trust me and won't buy.
intake_responses.current_plan: I'm starting to ask for a small non-refundable deposit on mobile money before I dispatch, to filter out the non-serious buyers. I'm also building reviews and testimonials so new customers trust me enough to pay upfront.

intake_responses.business_description: I grow tomatoes, onions and green vegetables on my farm near Jinja and sell them fresh. I take them to the market myself and also supply a few hotels and food vendors in town.
intake_responses.customers: Market vendors who buy to resell, hotels and restaurants wanting fresh supply, and individual households who come to the farm. Tomatoes are my biggest earner when the price is right.
intake_responses.competitors: Many farmers grow tomatoes here, so when the season is good the market is flooded and prices collapse. There are also tomatoes trucked in from other regions that compete with mine.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I earn from selling the harvest at market and the supply deals with hotels. The hotel supply is smaller but more reliable than the open market.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest challenge is that tomatoes spoil so fast and I have no way to preserve or add value to them. When the market is flooded I can't sell fast enough and watch crates rot within days, forcing me to almost give them away. I hear people make tomato paste and sauce but I don't know how, and I don't have the equipment or knowledge to process them. So all my hard work rots when supply is high, while in the dry season I have nothing to sell.
intake_responses.current_plan: I'm trying to time my planting so I harvest slightly off-season when prices are higher and there's less competition. I'm also curious about learning simple processing like drying or making sauce to save the excess instead of losing it.

intake_responses.business_description: I sell fresh produce, matoke, tomatoes, onions and greens at Kalerwe market. I buy early morning from the trucks that come from the villages and sell throughout the day at my spot.
intake_responses.customers: Households buying food for home, small restaurants and kibanda owners buying in slightly bigger quantities, and passers-by. I have some regulars who come to me because they trust my prices.
intake_responses.competitors: The whole of Kalerwe is produce sellers, we're packed side by side selling the exact same matoke and tomatoes. Customers just walk past comparing, so if my price is even slightly higher they move to the next person.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I earn from the small margin between what I buy from the trucks and what I sell during the day. It's high volume, small profit on each item.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest struggle is that I buy from the trucks before I even know the price customers will accept that day, and prices swing wildly. Some mornings I buy matoke expecting to sell high, but that same day many trucks come and the market floods, so I'm forced to sell at almost what I paid or watch it rot. I'm gambling every dawn on prices I can't predict, and one bad guess wipes out days of profit. The perishable nature means I can't wait for a better price.
intake_responses.current_plan: I'm trying to build relationships with a couple of truck drivers so I get first news of how much produce is coming that day. I'm also learning to buy less on days that look oversupplied instead of stocking too much.

intake_responses.business_description: I run a small events and photography business in Mbarara, covering weddings, graduations, introductions and birthdays. I have two cameras, some lighting, and I hire extra help for big events.
intake_responses.customers: Couples getting married, families doing traditional introduction ceremonies, students at graduation, and businesses wanting photos for promotion. Most come during the wedding and graduation seasons.
intake_responses.competitors: There are many photographers now since anyone with a good camera or even a phone calls themselves a photographer. Some undercut me badly with very low prices, and clients often don't see the quality difference until after the event.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I earn per event package, which includes the shooting, editing and delivering photos and videos. Bigger weddings bring the most money.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest problem is that this business is deeply seasonal, everything happens around December, and the wedding and introduction months, then for long stretches there's almost nothing. During the busy season I sometimes double-book or can't handle all the clients, but for months after I sit with expensive equipment and no income while it depreciates. I can't smooth it out, so I feast then starve, and I struggle to keep my hired helpers who leave for other work in the dry months.
intake_responses.current_plan: I'm trying to add services that aren't seasonal, like product photography for businesses and passport photos, to earn during the quiet months. I'm also thinking of offering photo printing and framing to keep some steady cash between events.

intake_responses.business_description: I brew and sell local drinks, mostly tonto and a bit of malwa, from my place near Fort Portal, and I also cook local food to sell alongside so people eat while they drink. It's a busy spot in the evenings.
intake_responses.customers: Mostly men from the neighbourhood, farmers coming from their gardens, and boda riders who stop by after work. They come in the evenings and on weekends to relax and drink.
intake_responses.competitors: There are several other tonto and malwa places around, and the bottled beer and waragi are also competing for the same drinkers who have a little more money. Some of my regulars switch to whoever's brew is fresher and stronger.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I earn from selling the drinks by the cup or jerrycan and from the food I sell to those drinking. The weekend evenings bring the bulk of my money.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest struggle is that so many of my customers drink on credit, promising to pay after their harvest or at month-end, and I keep giving because they're my regulars and I fear losing them. But my book of debtors keeps growing and much of it I never recover, so I'm brewing and serving with my own money and not getting it all back. When I try to refuse credit, they go drink at the next place, but continuing like this I'm slowly draining my capital. I'm too soft and it's costing me.
intake_responses.current_plan: I'm trying to set a small limit on how much credit each person can take before they must clear. I'm also starting to note debts in a book in front of them so they feel accountable, and encouraging cash by giving a tiny extra to those who pay immediately.

intake_responses.business_description: I sell electronics accessories in Wandegeya, phone chargers, power banks, earphones, Bluetooth speakers and cables. I have a small lockable stall and I also sell to a few people online through WhatsApp status.
intake_responses.customers: University students mostly, since Makerere is near, and young workers. They want cheap but decent accessories, and the students buy a lot at the start of semester.
intake_responses.competitors: There are so many stalls selling the same chargers and earphones right around me. And now people order the same things from online sellers and Jumia sometimes cheaper, so my walk-in customers are reducing.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I earn on the markup of each item. Power banks and speakers give better margins than the small cables and earphones.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest challenge is that my sales completely die during the university holidays. When students go home, Wandegeya empties out and for two or three months my daily sales drop by more than half, but I'm still paying rent every month regardless. I built my whole business around the students without realising how dependent I am on them being here. During holidays I sometimes can't even cover rent and eat into my stock money. I need customers who are here all year, not just in semester.
intake_responses.current_plan: I'm thinking of pushing my online WhatsApp sales harder so I can reach customers beyond Wandegeya who buy even during holidays. I'm also considering stocking items that non-students need, like household electronics, to balance the seasons.

intake_responses.business_description: I do agro-processing making groundnut paste, what we call odii, and I also mill and package simmsim. I buy raw nuts from farmers around Lira, process them, and sell in packets to shops and individuals.
intake_responses.customers: Shops and supermarkets in Lira that stock my packets, households who buy directly, and some traders who carry my paste to Kampala. NGOs sometimes order in bulk for their programs.
intake_responses.competitors: Many women make groundnut paste at home and sell it loose, cheaper than my packaged one. There are also bigger brands with nice packaging in supermarkets that customers trust more than my small label.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I earn from selling the packaged paste and simsim. The packaged product sells for more than loose, and bulk orders bring good lump sums when they come.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest problem is that the quality of my paste changes depending on the groundnuts I get, and I can't always get good clean nuts. Sometimes the farmers bring nuts that are moldy or not well dried, and if I process those the paste tastes off or spoils fast, and then shops return it and my reputation suffers. But if I reject bad nuts, I don't have enough raw material to keep producing steadily. Sorting them properly takes so much time and I still can't tell some of the bad ones until it's too late.
intake_responses.current_plan: I'm trying to train and pay a bit more to a few reliable farmers to dry and sort their nuts properly before selling to me. I'm also thinking of getting a moisture meter or better drying so I can control quality before processing.

intake_responses.business_description: I sell second-hand clothes, what we call mivumba, here in Owino. I buy bales from the importers and sort them, then sell the good pieces to customers walking through the market. I have been doing this for about six years now.
intake_responses.customers: Mostly young women looking for cheap but nice dresses and tops. Some resellers also come to buy from me in small quantities to sell in their villages upcountry.
intake_responses.competitors: Eh, there are so many of us selling mivumba in Owino, you cannot count. The person next to me sells the same thing, so it is really about who calls the customer first and who gives a better price.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I make money selling the clothes piece by piece. On a good day I can get maybe 80,000 to 120,000 shillings, but it depends on how the bale was.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest problem is the bales themselves. When I open a bale I have already paid for, sometimes half of it is torn or stained clothes that nobody will buy. I never know what I am getting until I have already spent my money, so some weeks I lose badly.
intake_responses.current_plan: I am thinking of finding a supplier who lets me see inside before I pay, but those ones charge more. I also want to start washing and repairing some of the damaged pieces to sell them cheaper instead of throwing them away.

intake_responses.business_description: I run a phone repair shop near Gulu Main Market. I fix cracked screens, change batteries, and do software flashing for people whose phones are stuck. I trained myself mostly from YouTube and from working under another technician.
intake_responses.customers: All kinds of people, from students to boda riders to business people. Anyone with a broken phone comes to me because I am cheaper than taking it to the official shops in Kampala.
intake_responses.competitors: There are maybe four other repair guys around here. Some of them are cheaper but they do bad work, so customers come back to me after being disappointed by them.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I charge for the repair plus the cost of the spare part. Screens are where I make most money because they break a lot, especially the Tecno and itel phones people use here.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest challenge is getting genuine spare parts. The screens I buy from Kampala suppliers sometimes fail within two weeks, and then the customer blames me and refuses to pay again. I cannot always tell which parts are good until they are already installed and start failing.
intake_responses.current_plan: I want to build a relationship with one trusted supplier in Kampala instead of buying from whoever is cheapest. I am also thinking of giving a short warranty so customers trust me more, but that is risky if the parts keep failing.

intake_responses.business_description: I have a small juice bar in Naalya where I make fresh juices from passion fruit, mango, and beetroot. I also do smoothies for the gym people nearby. I started after finishing my degree because there were no jobs.
intake_responses.customers: Mostly office workers and people from the gym close by. They like the healthy natural juices, no added sugar. Weekends I get families passing by.
intake_responses.competitors: There is a supermarket nearby selling packaged juices which are cheaper, and one other lady with a stall. But mine is fresh, so the health-conscious ones prefer me.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I sell each bottle between 3,000 and 6,000 shillings depending on the size. Most people pay by MTN mobile money now, very few use cash.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest struggle is that my fruits go bad so quickly and I cannot predict how many customers will come each day. If I buy plenty and few people come, I lose the fruit. If I buy little and many come, I run out and disappoint them and they go to the supermarket.
intake_responses.current_plan: I am trying to keep records of how much I sell each day to guess better, but the numbers jump around too much. I also thought about taking pre-orders through WhatsApp so I know how much to prepare in the morning.

intake_responses.business_description: I keep dairy cows on my land outside Mbarara and I bring the milk to sell in town every morning. I have twelve cows now. I supply some to a milk collection center and sell the rest directly to households and small shops.
intake_responses.customers: Households who want fresh milk daily, plus two restaurants and a few small shops that resell it. The collection center takes the bigger volume but pays less per litre.
intake_responses.competitors: Many farmers around Mbarara keep cows, this is cattle country. So there is always plenty of milk, especially in rainy season, and prices fall because everybody is selling.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I sell milk per litre. The collection center gives me maybe 1,000 shillings a litre but direct customers pay 1,500. The direct sales are better but I cannot sell everything that way.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest problem is that in the rainy season the cows produce so much milk that the price crashes because everyone has plenty, but in dry season I have little milk to sell even though the price is high. So I never seem to make good money at the same time as having plenty to sell.
intake_responses.current_plan: I am thinking of making yoghurt or ghee from the extra rainy-season milk so it does not go to waste, but I do not have the equipment or knowledge yet. I also want to plant more grass to feed cows in dry season so they keep producing.

intake_responses.business_description: I sell electronics in Mbale town, things like phone chargers, earphones, power banks, and small speakers. I import some from Kampala dealers and sell them from my small shop. I have been open three years.
intake_responses.customers: Young people and students mostly. Also people who need cheap chargers because theirs got spoiled. Boda riders buy phone holders and chargers from me too.
intake_responses.competitors: There are several shops on my street selling the same accessories. We all buy from the same Kampala suppliers so our stock is almost identical, which makes it hard to stand out.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I add a markup on each item. Power banks give me the most profit but they are also the most expensive to stock, so my money gets tied up in them.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest challenge is that all of us on this street sell exactly the same items at almost the same price, so customers just walk to whoever is closest or slightly cheaper. I cannot raise my prices and I cannot easily get different stock without more capital, so I feel stuck fighting over the same customers.
intake_responses.current_plan: I am considering stocking one or two unique items nobody else has, maybe better quality branded chargers, so people come to me specifically. But I worry the market here is too price-sensitive to pay more for quality.

intake_responses.business_description: I run a salon in Wandegeya doing hair plaiting, braids, weaves, and nails. I have two girls working with me. Students from Makerere are a big part of my business since we are close to campus.
intake_responses.customers: Mostly female university students and some working ladies. During exam time and holidays it changes a lot because students go home.
intake_responses.competitors: So many salons in Wandegeya, it is one of the most crowded areas for this. Some are newer and fancier with air conditioning which pulls the students who want the modern look.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I charge per style. Braids are the biggest earner, maybe 40,000 to 80,000 depending on the style and the hair. Nails and simple plaiting bring smaller amounts.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest problem is that my two workers keep leaving to start their own salons or move to fancier ones, and they take some of my regular customers with them because clients follow the person who does their hair. So I keep training people and then losing them and my customer base too.
intake_responses.current_plan: I am thinking of paying my best girls a share of what they bring in so they feel like partners and stay. I also want to build the salon's own reputation on Instagram so customers come for the salon name, not just one person.

intake_responses.business_description: I run an IT training center in Gulu teaching computer basics, Microsoft Office, and internet skills to young people and adults. I have eight computers and I run classes in shifts. Many of my students are looking for office jobs or NGO work.
intake_responses.customers: Young people who finished school and need computer certificates to get jobs, plus some older civil servants told by their offices to get computer skills. NGO staff also come for specific training.
intake_responses.competitors: There are two other training centers in Gulu, but I think mine is more organized. The bigger issue is people learning from phones and YouTube now instead of paying for a class.
intake_responses.revenue_source: Students pay per course, usually a two or three month program. I charge around 150,000 shillings for the full package with a certificate at the end.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest struggle is that students pay for the course, come for the first few weeks, then disappear before finishing and before paying the balance. I have already used my computers and electricity on them but I never collect the full fee, so my income is always less than my enrollment suggests.
intake_responses.current_plan: I am considering asking for full payment upfront, but then fewer people would enroll because they do not have all the money at once. Maybe I can break it into weekly payments tied to attendance so they must pay to continue.

intake_responses.business_description: I sell chapati and rolex on the roadside in Kalerwe near the market. Early morning and evening are my busy times when people are going to and from work. I have my little stall with a charcoal stove.
intake_responses.customers: Workers passing by, boda riders, students, and people who do not want to cook. Everyone loves a hot rolex, so I get all kinds of people.
intake_responses.competitors: There are other rolex sellers around, maybe five within walking distance. We all charge about the same, 1,500 for a plain one, 2,000 with an egg and extras.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I sell each rolex and chapati for cash mostly. On a good evening I can make maybe 60,000 shillings but the flour, eggs, and charcoal eat into it a lot.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest problem is that the price of cooking oil and eggs keeps jumping up without warning, but my customers refuse to accept if I raise my price even by 200 shillings. So when costs go up my profit disappears completely, and I cannot pass it on to the customer.
intake_responses.current_plan: I am trying to buy oil and flour in bigger quantities when the price is low to protect myself, but I do not have enough money to stock up much. I also thought of adding sausages and other extras that give better profit than plain rolex.

intake_responses.business_description: I do carpentry and furniture making in Jinja. I make beds, wardrobes, chairs, and tables on order. I have a small workshop and two young men helping me. I have been in this trade over fifteen years.
intake_responses.customers: People setting up new homes, landlords furnishing rentals, and some hotels and guesthouses in Jinja that need furniture. Most orders are custom made to what the customer wants.
intake_responses.competitors: There are many carpenters in Jinja and cheaper imported furniture from China is coming into the shops now, which pulls some customers who want fast and cheap over quality.
intake_responses.revenue_source: Customers pay per item made, usually a deposit first and the balance on delivery. A good wardrobe can bring 400,000 to 700,000 depending on the wood and design.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest challenge is that customers pay a small deposit, I use it plus my own money to buy timber and start the work, then when it is finished they delay paying the balance for weeks or months. My money gets stuck in furniture sitting in the workshop, so I cannot start new orders.
intake_responses.current_plan: I want to insist on at least half payment before starting, but customers say other carpenters accept smaller deposits so I lose the job. Maybe I can make some standard items ready-made so I am not always waiting on custom order payments.

intake_responses.business_description: I run a wholesale shop in Kikuubo selling household items like plastic basins, buckets, cups, and jerrycans. I buy in bulk from importers and sell to retailers who come from upcountry to stock their village shops.
intake_responses.customers: Small shop owners from all over Uganda who come to Kikuubo to buy in bulk. Some individual customers too but mostly resellers buying by the carton.
intake_responses.competitors: Kikuubo is packed with wholesalers doing the same thing. Everyone is competing on price and giving credit to keep the resellers coming back to them instead of the neighbor.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I make a small margin on each carton but sell in large volumes. The profit per item is thin so I depend on moving a lot of stock quickly.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest problem is that to keep my upcountry customers I have to sell to them on credit, but then some of them delay or fail to pay after they have taken the goods back to their villages far away. Chasing them is hard and expensive, and I have already restocked using money I do not actually have yet.
intake_responses.current_plan: I am thinking of only giving credit to customers I have known for a long time and requiring new ones to pay cash. I also want to track who owes me properly instead of keeping it in my head, because I lose count and forget who has not paid.

intake_responses.business_description: I keep poultry, mostly layers for eggs, on the outskirts of Lira. I have about 500 birds now. I sell eggs to shops and hotels in Lira town and sometimes the spent hens for meat.
intake_responses.customers: Retail shops, restaurants, and hotels in Lira that need eggs regularly. A few individuals come directly to my farm to buy trays cheaper.
intake_responses.competitors: There are other poultry farmers around Lira, and sometimes cheaper eggs come in from Kampala farms which undercut our local price.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I sell eggs by the tray, usually around 11,000 to 13,000 shillings a tray depending on the season. The steady demand from shops keeps me going.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest challenge is the cost of feed, which is the biggest expense in this business. The feed prices keep rising and sometimes the quality is poor so my hens lay fewer eggs, but I still paid full price for that bad feed. I cannot always tell if it is the feed, disease, or something else causing the drop.
intake_responses.current_plan: I am thinking of mixing my own feed using local maize and sunflower to cut costs, but I am not sure of the right formula and I fear getting the nutrition wrong. I might also test different feed suppliers to see which gives better laying.

intake_responses.business_description: I run a small restaurant near Amber Court in Jinja serving local food like matoke, posho, beans, rice, and meat at lunchtime. I mostly serve office workers and people working in the town center.
intake_responses.customers: Office workers, shop attendants, and passersby who come for lunch. It is very busy from 12 to 2pm and then quiet the rest of the day.
intake_responses.competitors: There are several local restaurants nearby offering the same kind of food at similar prices. Competition is high at lunchtime, everyone wants the same customers.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I charge per plate, around 5,000 to 8,000 shillings depending on the meat. Most of my money comes in that two-hour lunch rush.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest struggle is that almost all my business happens in those two lunch hours, and the rest of the day my staff and my rent are just costing me money while I earn nothing. I have tried opening for supper but very few people come in the evening in this area, so I am paying for a full day but only earning for two hours.
intake_responses.current_plan: I am considering doing takeaway deliveries to nearby offices to spread out my sales, or maybe doing breakfast for early workers. I also thought of renting a smaller place, but then I would lose my good lunchtime location.

intake_responses.business_description: I install and sell solar systems for homes and small businesses, mostly in areas around Kampala with poor power. I do the panels, batteries, and lights, and I service them when they have problems. I studied electrical engineering.
intake_responses.customers: Households in areas with bad electricity, small shops, and some people building homes upcountry who want backup power. Also poultry farmers who need reliable lighting.
intake_responses.competitors: There are big solar companies with cheaper imported kits, and also cheap fake products in the market that fail quickly. Customers cannot tell the difference until it stops working.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I make money on selling the equipment plus the installation labor. A full home system can be 1.5 to 3 million shillings. Servicing brings smaller repeat income.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest problem is that customers compare my quality systems to the cheap fake ones in the market and think I am overcharging, because on the surface the panels look the same. They buy the cheap one, it fails in a year, and then they distrust all solar including mine, so I lose the whole market not just one sale.
intake_responses.current_plan: I am thinking of offering a longer warranty and maybe letting customers pay in installments through mobile money so the higher price feels manageable. I also want to educate customers on how to spot fake products, but that is slow work.

intake_responses.business_description: I sell shoes in Gulu Main Market, both new imported ones and some second-hand. Ladies' shoes, men's, and children's. I have a stall and I display them on a table outside.
intake_responses.customers: All kinds of people needing shoes, but especially during school opening when parents buy for children, and around Christmas when everyone wants new shoes.
intake_responses.competitors: Many shoe sellers in the market with similar stock. We compete a lot during the busy seasons but in between we all struggle for the few customers.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I mark up each pair. Children's shoes sell fast during school time, and I make good money during the holiday rush, but it is uneven across the year.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest challenge is that my sales are completely tied to school terms and Christmas. During those weeks I sell so much I run out of stock, but in the middle of the term months can pass with barely any sales while my money is tied up in shoes nobody is buying, and I still have to eat and pay rent.
intake_responses.current_plan: I am thinking of stocking cheaper everyday sandals and work shoes that people buy anytime, not just for occasions, to smooth out the slow months. I also want to save more during the busy season so I survive the dry periods better.

intake_responses.business_description: I do boda-boda transport in Soroti, carrying people and small goods around town and to nearby villages. I own two motorcycles now, one I ride and one another young man rides and pays me daily.
intake_responses.customers: People needing quick transport around town, market women moving goods, students, and people going to villages where taxis do not reach easily.
intake_responses.competitors: So many boda riders in Soroti, it is one of the most common jobs. We compete at the stages for passengers, and now those app boda things from Kampala are talked about but not really here yet.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I earn from fares each day, plus the fixed amount my rider pays me for the second bike. Fuel and repairs take a big chunk of what I earn.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest problem is the young man riding my second bike. Some days he claims he made very little, other days the bike develops problems I suspect come from careless riding, and I have no way to know if he is telling me the truth or keeping money and abusing my machine. My second bike costs me more in repairs than it earns.
intake_responses.current_plan: I am thinking of switching to a fixed daily payment where he keeps whatever extra he makes, so he takes better care of the bike and I do not have to trust his daily figures. I also want to save to buy him out into a hire-purchase so he owns it eventually.

intake_responses.business_description: I bake cakes and mandazi from home in Mbale and supply them to shops and take orders for birthdays and weddings. I started small in my mother's kitchen and now I have a proper oven.
intake_responses.customers: Shops that buy my mandazi to resell, plus individuals who order cakes for celebrations. Word of mouth brings me most of my cake orders.
intake_responses.competitors: Other home bakers in Mbale and a couple of proper bakeries in town. The bakeries have machines and can make more, but people say my cakes taste better and are more personal.
intake_responses.revenue_source: Cakes bring the most money, a celebration cake can be 60,000 to 200,000 shillings. The mandazi supply is small but steady daily income.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest struggle is that when I get a big cake order I sometimes cannot handle it because I am also doing the daily mandazi and I only have one small oven and myself. I have turned down wedding orders because I could not manage the volume in time, so I am losing the most profitable business because I cannot scale up my baking.
intake_responses.current_plan: I am thinking of hiring one person to help with the mandazi so I focus on cakes, and maybe saving for a second bigger oven. But I fear taking on staff cost when my income is not steady enough yet.

intake_responses.business_description: I do agro-processing, specifically grinding and packaging maize flour and also groundnut paste, in Mbarara. I buy maize and groundnuts from farmers, process them, and sell packaged flour to shops and schools.
intake_responses.customers: Retail shops, boarding schools that need bulk flour for posho, and some households buying directly. Schools are my biggest and most reliable buyers.
intake_responses.competitors: There are bigger millers with branded packaging and also small millers who just grind for a fee. I sit in the middle trying to build my own brand.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I sell packaged flour and paste by weight. The school contracts give me bulk sales, and the branded retail flour gives better margins but sells slower.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest problem is that the maize I buy varies a lot in quality and moisture depending on which farmer and season, so my flour comes out different each time, sometimes finer, sometimes with a different color or taste. Schools and shops complain about the inconsistency, but I cannot always control what the farmers bring me.
intake_responses.current_plan: I am thinking of buying a moisture meter and setting standards for the maize I accept, maybe paying a bit more for consistent quality grain. I also want to dry and store maize properly myself so I control the input better instead of depending on whatever comes.

intake_responses.business_description: I am a tailor in Owino Market. I make and repair clothes, do school uniforms, and sew dresses and shirts to order. I have one sewing machine and an overlock machine. I trained at a vocational institute.
intake_responses.customers: People who want custom-made outfits, parents needing school uniforms, and walk-ins with clothes to repair or alter. I get busy before school opening and holidays.
intake_responses.competitors: Owino is full of tailors, we are lined up next to each other. Also ready-made mivumba clothes are so cheap that many people just buy those instead of tailoring new ones.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I charge per garment made or repaired. Uniforms in bulk before school opening are my biggest earner. Repairs bring small but steady money.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest challenge is that ready-made second-hand clothes are so cheap now that fewer people want to pay for tailoring a new dress, so I depend mostly on uniforms and repairs. But repairs pay very little and uniforms only come twice a year, so between those times I sit with my machines idle earning almost nothing.
intake_responses.current_plan: I am thinking of specializing in something the mivumba cannot easily give, like fitted African-print outfits for events, which people pay more for. I also want to advertise on WhatsApp status to reach customers beyond just those walking through Owino.

intake_responses.business_description: I sell agricultural inputs in Gulu, things like seeds, fertilizer, pesticides, and farming tools. Farmers come to me before planting seasons to buy what they need for their gardens.
intake_responses.customers: Small-scale farmers around Gulu, some cooperatives, and a few NGOs that buy inputs for farmer programs. Demand comes strongly at the start of each planting season.
intake_responses.competitors: There are a few other agro-input shops in Gulu, and sometimes NGOs distribute free seeds and inputs which reduces what farmers buy from us that season.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I make a margin on each product. Fertilizer and quality seeds sell in volume at planting time, and I earn most of my yearly income in those planting windows.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest problem is that all my sales are squeezed into the two planting seasons, and I have to stock up a lot of inputs beforehand using borrowed money. But if the rains come late or fail, farmers do not plant and do not buy, and I am left with expired chemicals and seeds while still owing the loan I used to stock them.
intake_responses.current_plan: I am thinking of stocking more non-perishable items like tools that do not expire, so weather does not ruin my stock. I also want to arrange with suppliers to return unsold inputs, but they usually refuse that arrangement.

intake_responses.business_description: I run a small coffee shop and eatery in Fort Portal serving coffee, tea, snacks, and light meals. Fort Portal grows a lot of coffee so I try to serve good local coffee to tourists and locals.
intake_responses.customers: Tourists passing through Fort Portal on the way to the parks, some NGO workers, and local professionals. Weekends and tourist season are much busier.
intake_responses.competitors: A few other cafes and the hotels that also serve coffee. The hotels have more visibility with tourists because visitors stay there and eat there.
intake_responses.revenue_source: Coffee, meals, and snacks sold to customers. Tourists spend more per visit, but locals give me the steady weekday trade even if they spend less.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest struggle is that my busy times depend heavily on tourists coming to the parks, and that rises and falls with the tourism seasons and things outside my control like travel news. When tourists are few, I lean on locals, but locals do not spend enough to cover my costs, so my income swings wildly and I cannot plan or hire steadily.
intake_responses.current_plan: I am thinking of building a stronger local customer base with things locals want, like affordable lunch specials and a nice place to work with wifi, so I depend less on tourists. I also want to sell packaged local coffee beans that tourists can take home.

intake_responses.business_description: I sell and repair computers and laptops in Kikuubo, mostly used ones imported from abroad. I test them, fix any problems, install software, and sell them to students and small offices.
intake_responses.customers: University students needing affordable laptops, small businesses, and people who cannot afford brand-new machines. Also some who bring their laptops for repair.
intake_responses.competitors: Many dealers in the same building selling used laptops from the same import sources, so prices are very competitive and everyone claims their machines are best.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I make a margin on each laptop sold plus repair fees. The used laptops move well but the profit per unit keeps getting thinner as more dealers join.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest problem is that the used laptops I import are unpredictable, some arrive with hidden faults like bad batteries or failing hard drives that only show after the customer has used them for a while. Then they come back angry demanding refunds, and I lose both the sale and my reputation, but I could not have known the fault when I sold it.
intake_responses.current_plan: I am thinking of testing each machine more thoroughly and running it for a few days before selling, but that ties up my money longer. I also want to offer a short warranty and build trust, and maybe find a more reliable importer even if it costs more.

intake_responses.business_description: I sell fresh produce in Kalerwe market, mostly greens like dodo, nakati, sukuma, and tomatoes and onions. I buy from farmers who bring produce to the market early and sell it retail throughout the day.
intake_responses.customers: Households buying for their daily cooking, plus some small restaurant owners who come to stock vegetables. Kalerwe is a busy market so I get good foot traffic.
intake_responses.competitors: So many vegetable sellers in Kalerwe, we are packed together selling the same greens. Prices are almost the same for everyone so it comes down to freshness and who calls the customer.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I sell greens in small heaps and tomatoes and onions by the cup or heap. Small amounts but many customers each day. Cash mostly.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest challenge is that I have to buy the greens fresh each morning, but I cannot predict exactly how many customers will come, so if I buy too much the greens wilt by evening and I throw them away at a loss. If I buy too little I run out and customers go to the seller next to me. I lose either way.
intake_responses.current_plan: I am thinking of buying less in the morning and topping up around midday if sales are good, since farmers keep bringing produce. I also want to sell the near-wilting greens cheaply in the evening rather than throwing them away completely.

intake_responses.business_description: I run a hardware and building materials shop in Mbarara selling cement, iron sheets, nails, paint, and pipes. People building homes and contractors are my main customers.
intake_responses.customers: Individuals building their own homes, small contractors, and hardware resellers in smaller towns nearby. Construction picks up when people have money after harvests.
intake_responses.competitors: Several hardware shops in Mbarara selling the same brands like Tororo cement and Roofings iron sheets. Everyone stocks the same big brands so it is hard to differentiate.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I sell building materials with a margin. Cement moves in volume but with thin margins, while paint and fittings give better profit per item.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest problem is that big items like cement and iron sheets tie up huge amounts of my capital sitting in the store, and prices from the manufacturers change often, so sometimes I buy a big stock and then the price drops and my competitors sell cheaper than what I paid. I am always guessing when to stock up and when to hold back.
intake_responses.current_plan: I am thinking of keeping less cement in stock and reordering more frequently even if transport costs more, to avoid getting stuck with expensive stock. I also want to focus more on the smaller high-margin items where my money is not so exposed to price swings.

intake_responses.business_description: I run a small local eatery in Wandegeya serving affordable food to students, things like katogo in the morning, rice and beans, matoke, and chicken on request. I cook everything fresh daily.
intake_responses.customers: Mostly Makerere students and some workers around Wandegeya. Students want filling food that is cheap, so my portions and prices matter a lot to them.
intake_responses.competitors: Many other student eateries around Wandegeya offering the same cheap local food. We all fight for the student budget which is very tight and price-sensitive.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I sell food per plate, keeping prices low like 3,500 to 5,000 so students can afford. I depend on high numbers of customers rather than big margins.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest struggle is that my customers are students, and when the university closes for holidays or during strikes and lockdowns, Wandegeya empties out completely and my sales collapse for weeks. I have staff and rent to pay year-round but my customers disappear for months at a time, and I have no other type of customer to fall back on.
intake_responses.current_plan: I am thinking of finding non-student customers like nearby office workers and shop attendants so I am not fully dependent on the university calendar. I also want to try lunchtime deliveries to offices during the holidays when students are gone.

intake_responses.business_description: I run a printing and stationery business in Lira offering printing, photocopying, lamination, and internet browsing. I also sell stationery and help people fill online forms like job applications and government services.
intake_responses.customers: Students, job seekers filling online applications, small businesses needing documents printed, and people applying for government services online who do not have computers themselves.
intake_responses.competitors: A few other printing shops in Lira offering the same services. Also more people now have smartphones and can do some things themselves, which reduces some of my browsing customers.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I charge per page for printing and copying, and fees for helping with online applications. The online form-filling service earns well because people cannot do it themselves.
intake_responses.main_challenge: My biggest problem is the unreliable internet and power in Lira. When the power goes off or the network is down, I cannot print or help anyone, and customers who came for urgent things like deadline applications get angry and go elsewhere. I lose the busiest moments precisely when the infrastructure fails, and I cannot control when that happens.
intake_responses.current_plan: I am thinking of buying a small generator or solar backup and a stronger router or multiple network SIMs so I am not stuck when one fails. But the cost is high and I am not sure the extra business will cover it, so I am still weighing it.
